News.title: Boyfriend, 18, ‘stabbed football star girlfriend to death before his mum helped hide body in back of blood-stained Jeep’
News.content:
'MY SON TOOK A LIFE' Boyfriend, 18, ‘stabbed football star girlfriend to death before his mum helped hide body in back of blood-stained Jeep’

A TEEN boy allegedly stabbed his girlfriend to death before enlisting his mother’s help to hide her body in the back of a bloodied car, cops reveal.

Karoline Heintz was found dead in the rear hatch of her Jeep Cherokee just outside the Pennsylvania Western University campus in California, Pennsylvania.



It is alleged her boyfriend, Royce Moser, 18, stabbed her to death.

Heintz’s family had contacted police for a welfare check after she failed to return to campus as expected on Wednesday.



The cops located her Cherokee near a library where they noticed some blood inside before finding her body.

She had multiple stab wounds – many in the chest – court documents reveal.

Royce Moser, 18, is facing a charge of criminal homicide in the death of Karoline Heintz, who played soccer for PennWest California.

During a press conference, Pennsylvania State Trooper Rocco Gagliardi said: “They’re a younger couple talking about how relationships can continue maybe in a college setting.



“Somewhere that conversation probably goes a little bit south.

“Towards the end of that conversation between boyfriend and girlfriend, he goes inside and grabs a large knife from the kitchen.”

The teen allegedly told Heintz he had something for her, allowing him to run inside and grab the weapon.

In a subsequent police interview, Royce said he had a “demon take over” him.

After the stabbing it is understood Heintz’s body fell from the car before Royce dragged her to the trunk, court documents reveal.



He then allegedly called his mother for help moving the car.

When his mother arrived, she told him to pull the car into the garage and they would clean it with disinfectant, police said.

She then reportedly gave him latex gloves and told him to follow her car.

While together on the way home after ditching the car off, Royce Moser allegedly admitted to his mother that he “stabbed the victim with a knife from his house.”

When they got back to the mother’s home, she told her son to “take a bath and then shower” and change his clothes, police said.



She put the knife in a garbage bag to be thrown out with the trash outside her home and washed his clothes.

Police later executed a search warrant at Rachel’s home and located a chef’s knife in a garbage bag, according to court documents.

Gagliardi continued: “It is more of an unfortunate event, 18-year-old girl, young soccer star ready to explore life, ready to start college, now can no longer get to do that.”

Royce and his mother were arrested on Thursday morning.

Moser was charged with criminal homicide, two counts of tampering with evidence, two counts of abuse of a corpse and obstruction.



His 57-year-old mother was charged with tampering, obstruction, hindering the apprehension of a fugitive and abuse of a corpse.

She told reporters she was sorry “that my son took a life.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The school said in a statement: “PennWest University is deeply saddened by the tragic death of Karoline Heintz, who was a first-year student at the California campus.

“Our heartfelt condolences go out to her family, friends, and all those affected by this tragedy.”

News.title: Brave officers killed in tragic crash are pictured after five ‘joyriders’ drove wrong way down A66 during chase
News.content:
TWO cops who died in a crash on the A66 after their police car smashed into another vehicle driving the wrong way have been pictured.

PC Matthew Blades, 37 and PC Tom Clough, 38, were killed alongside five “joyriders” when they collided with a Volkswagen Passat following a police chase.



The police officers and all five occupants of the Passat were declared dead at the scene following the early-hours crash near Middlesbrough.

The two brave police officers killed in the horror collision have now been named and pictured and tributes have flooded in.



The youngsters have been named as Michael Cahill, 23, Theo Rae, 17. Cole Worthy, 17, Jacob Matusiak, 23, and Makai Saddington, 18.

The VW is understood to have been using cloned plates and was first picked up by an ANPR camera.

PC Clough is understood to have served as a soldier in Britain’s military operations in Iraq and Afghanistan before later becoming a Cleveland Police officer.

Former comrades have paid tribute to the “fantastic soldier” and “true friend”, with many taking to social media to share their pride at having served alongside him.



His heartbroken family said he was “our hero” with a “fantastic sense of humour”.

They added: “He jumped into action whenever needed, and was willing to help anyone for any reason.

“He proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place.

“He was always on public duty throughout his short life.

“We as a family and Tom’s partner would like to express our sincere gratitude for the overwhelming support and condolences from friends, colleagues and the wider community.”



Police officers then started a a high-speed chase in the early hours of Saturday morning.

They followed the car though Middlesbrough for just under seven minutes before the pursuit was halted when the VW joined the A66 against the flow of traffic.

Just 10 seconds later, at 3.39am the car ploughed into another marked armed-response vehicle carrying the two PCs which was travelling on the correct side of the carriageway.



Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said yesterday afternoon: “This is an incredibly sad day for Cleveland.

“The loss has been felt across our communities, by our police family and by our partner agencies.”

She said the tragic pair “were brave officers protecting our communities and serving our residents who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift”.

Chief Constable Fuller said she has visited the families of both officers to “offer our condolences and support”.

An investigation has been launched into the crash by the Independent Office for Police Conduct.



PC Matty Blades was a youth coach at Seaton Carew Football Club in Hartlepool.

The club are flying their flags at half mast and paid tribute, saying: “It is with the heaviest of hearts that Seaton Carew FC shares the devastating news of the passing of one of our coaches, Matty, who tragically lost his life in a fatal accident while carrying out his duties as a police officer.



“Matty had only recently joined our club as a coach and was preparing for his first season with our brand-new U7 Seahawks team.

“He was looking forward to being part of the team and, most importantly, to coaching his own son, who is going to be playing for the Seahawks this season.

“Matty and his oldest son are much-loved member of our club and our U10 Lions football family.

“Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Matty’s wife, his two boys, and all of his family and friends at this incredibly difficult and heartbreaking time.

“We also stand alongside Matty’s colleagues and friends within the police service, who have tragically lost members of their force.



“From everyone at Seaton Carew FC, thank you, Matty, for choosing to become part of our club. You will always be remembered as one of our own.Rest peacefully, Matty.

“Forever a part of the Seaton Carew FC family.”

Footage has also shown the moment two police cars pursued a suspect down a narrow road minutes before the tragedy unfolded.

Residents living on Lime Road, a mile from the crash site, said they woke to the sound of screeching tyres just after 3.30am on Saturday.



Ellie Westerman, 24, said: “The car must have been travelling at between 80 and 100 mph down our narrow street.

“The noise woke me and I shot out of bed, you could feel the vibration in the house as the car went past and the police vehicles followed with their lights and sirens going.

“It was frightening that cars were being driven at that speed through a residential area and it’s tragic people have ended up dying.”

One of the youngsters, Makai, previously posted several videos to TikTok which appear to show him in a high-speed police chase.

In one video, from months before his death teens can be seen driving through a housing estate at speed while a police car with blue flashing lights follows.



The Audi then peels off onto a grassy playing field in an attempt to lose the chase.

Another clip features a green Nissan being driven around before it is torched.

Images posted to the account show Saddington and a friend in black balaclavas posing in a car.



Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was “devastated” to hear of the deaths of two police officers and five members of the public after the horror crash.

He posted on X: “Devastated to hear that two police officers have lost their lives while on duty in Cleveland this morning, as well as five members of the public.

“My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of everyone involved, and with everyone at Cleveland Police.

“Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances. I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Redcar MP Anna Turley posted on X: “Two of the seven people who have lost their lives were Cleveland Police officers, on duty serving our community.”



She added: “They went to work to keep people safe, and they should have come home to their families.”

News.title: I was hired to write Kray Twins rival Eddie Richardson’s biography – dark secrets he shared before he targeted my family
News.content:
THE LAST GANGSTER I was hired to write Kray Twins rival Eddie Richardson’s biography – dark secrets he shared before he targeted my family

SO, EDDIE Richardson – last of the 1960s gangsters who ruled London through torture and intimidation – is dead.

He’d fallen out with most of his friends and enemies including his own crimelord brother, the much more charming and charismatic Charlie who was head of their Richardsons’ clan.



I had the misfortune to be hired to ghost write Eddie’s autobiography by one of London’s biggest publishers back in the early 2000s.

Eddie had just got out of prison after serving a stretch for his role in trying to bring millions of pounds worth of cocaine into the UK.



He was broke and needed to come up with something legit that would earn him a few bob. So, he turned to the only person he knew in ‘the media’ and through her managed to get an introduction to a publisher, which is where I came in.

Trouble was that despite being in prison for at least 30 years of his life, dear old Eddie had never read a book. He preferred knocking out childlike paintings on canvas that he believed would be worth a lot more than the ones his old nemesis Ronnie Kray had rustled up while serving his life sentence for the murder of a rival gangster.

But when Eddie realised he couldn’t live off his own art, he decided the easiest way to earn a crust and keep his parole officer happy was to tell his life story – well his version of his life story.

And that’s where this gets complicated because Eddie decided he could cop a £50,000 advance without breathing a word about the childhood abuse he suffered and the inside details of all the headline hitting crimes he’d committed alongside brother Charlie.



This happened to include torturing underworld enemies, which had led to the Richardsons being labelled the ‘most evil brothers in the underworld’ by the popular press at the time.

Having agreed to be his ghost, I sat down with Eddie, tape recorder in hand to start to interviewing him in chronological order. Eddie had a problem with the word ‘chronological’ because it sounded suspicious to him and he accused me of ‘taking the piss’ out of him by using it.

A LIFE OF CRIME - EDDIE RICHARDSON DIES AT 90 The London mobland boss, who led the fearsome Richardson gang with late brother Charlie, is understood to have passed away peacefully surrounded by family. Eddie, an enforcer in the 1950s and 1960s, developed a career as an after-dinner speaker and artist in later life. Born in Camberwell, South London, in 1936, Eddie started off working in the scrap metal industry. He and older brother Charlie went on to build an empire of clubs and businesses across South London. They expanded into Soho and made a fortune through blue movie cinemas and providing fruit machines and bouncers for other venues. The Richardson crew, also including “Mad” Frankie Fraser, were dubbed the Torture Gang with a reputation for sadistic punishments. They fought a deadly turf war with late East London villains Ronnie and Reggie Kray in the 1960s. The Krays got life for murder and Eddie and Charlie, who died aged 78 in 2012, also served long jail terms. He also worked with charities and boxing clubs. Eddie dismissed the Krays in an interview with The Sun last year, saying: “They were f***ing mugs. Very thick.” An underworld source said: “When people think of old-school gangsters, they think of the Krays. “But the Richardson gang were arguably more heavy-duty. “With Eddie passing, it’s the end of an era.”

When I explained that all it meant was that I was going to interview him about his childhood first, his face dropped and he gave me a death stare that must have no doubt scared the shit out of many of his victims.

“Why the f*** d’you want to know about my childhood?” he said, slowly to stop himself yelling at me.

“Well, Eddie. You’ve signed up to tell your life story, so that includes your early years.”



“F*** off,” he said. “I ain’t goin’ into that stuff. Let’s start with my first spell in borstal.”

I didn’t argue but I knew I’d have to make him go back to his childhood at some stage, otherwise I wouldn’t get my fee for being his ghost writer.

But unfortunately it all went downhill from then on.

Eddie didn’t really want to discuss anything in detail and if I dared to ask him for a specific date re an event, his eyes would narrow and he’d shake his head and say, ‘I don’t f***in’ keep a diary. What does it matter when it was?”

Eddie’s did eventually briefly talk about how much he hated his father who used to beat him and his brother and that he didn’t trust men because of that. This didn’t bode well for our working relationship and by asking him questions all the time I was also reminding him of the interrogations he’d experienced at the hands of Scotland Yard’s finest.



It was quickly becoming clear that we were never going to achieve what the publisher required, so I explained all this to the editor, including how Eddie clearly didn’t get on well with men and suggested she replace me with a female writer, who might stand more chance of squeezing some actual facts out of him.

This recommendation to change his ghost writer went ahead much to my relief. And in my last ever call to Eddie on a Saturday morning I promised I would return the photos he’d lent me that were intended to be used in a photo section in the centre of his autobiography.

He suddenly sounded very bothered by what I was saying. He seemed to have forgotten I had the photos and it really irritated him.



I thought nothing more about it, except to promise myself I would ensure they were delivered back to him on the following Monday morning.

The next morning – a Sunday – I left my home in West London to play football south of the city when my wife rang me on my mobile.

She said a strange, aggressive old man had turned up at the doorstep to my house, put his foot in the doorway so she couldn’t shut it and demanded the immediate return of those photos.

She worked out who he was and then very coolly invited him into the house where she insisted on making him a coffee and introduced him to my extremely senile mother-in-law who knew about as much about the Richardson’s as she did England’s one and only world cup victory in 1966.

My wife whispered into the phone that Eddie was completely thrown by her charming demeanor, but it was clear that unless I got back to the house rather soon then he might start ripping the place apart.



Needless to say, I returned double quick but as I drove back to the house, a chilling thought crossed my mind. Eddie must have been sitting in his car watching my house until I left earlier. And now he was alone in my house with my wife and mother-in-law. I’d been intimidated by him and he’d rightly presumed that I’d come back the moment I heard he was there.

I shot back, found the photos and gently escorted Eddie out of the front door before waiting and watching until he got in his car and drove away.

Six months later I was with another infamous old school criminal who was helping me with a book when I walked into a notorious villain’s pub in south London and there was Eddie at the bar.

My face dropped as I told the other villain about our ‘previous’. His on the spot advice was that I should go up to Eddie, say hello, shake his hand very quickly and then walk away without uttering another word.

It worked brilliantly. Before Eddie had a chance to get angry I’d gone but at least he knew I wasn’t scared of him. That was the crucial ingredient.



You see, old school villains like Eddie Richardson may have prided themselves on helping little old ladies across the street but you cross these type of characters at your peril.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

So farewell Eddie. No doubt the old criminals already down there in the other underworld (including your own brother) may well be out for revenge when you turn up. Just watch yer back old son, as they say.

WENSLEY CLARKSON is one of Britain’s best selling true crime authors.

News.title: I survived 9/11 but the stranger I met didn’t – his last words stuck with me…and I’ve finally delivered them to his sons
News.content:
IN the darkness of the World Trade Center’s North Tower on September 11, 2001, two strangers from New York – both in the emergency services – worked together, desperately trying to get trapped civilians to safety.

Firefighter Bill Spade made it out alive, while police officer John D’Allara tragically died as the building collapsed on him.



In the 25 minutes they knew each other, Bill and John laughed about being from opposite sides of New York – and “wrote their own obituaries” – as they battled to escape the crumbling North Tower.



“Well, here we are in the middle of this tragedy – one tower coming down and the other minutes away from coming down – and in a matter of moments, we’re working together, and we’re talking about our families,” Bill tells The Sun.

“My uncle lived up near where John lived. I had also been a police officer before I became a fireman, and we talked about each of us getting out of the academy at a similar time.”

John, 47, told Bill about his wife Carol and his two boys, then aged seven and two, while Bill spoke about his own wife Cynthia and their two young sons, each giving the other the information their families would need if only one made it home.

Less than half an hour later, Bill would become the only member of Staten Island’s Rescue Company 5 to survive the attacks, while John was killed when the North Tower collapsed.

Ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11, now-retired Bill has spoken exclusively to The Sun about that horrific day, and the emotional moment he finally sat down with John’s now-adult sons for the upcoming National Geographic documentary 9/11: Reunited.



Bill says: “He was thinking of his boys right to the very end.

“There were no lights on; it was completely pitch black. We were helping people out of the building and talking about his wife and two boys, and my wife and boys.”

When Bill first encountered John, he was stuck at the bottom of a stairwell with dozens of civilians unable to open the jammed doors standing between them and escape.

Bill says he most vividly remembers John’s calmness, even in the most terrifying circumstances.

“I was always proud of myself for being calm and cool in a situation and not letting emotions get the best of me, and I could certainly see that in John himself.”



The pair took turns charging at a door until they finally forced it open, allowing people to begin getting out.

“We left the North Tower about 30 seconds before it came down. John looked up and said, ‘It’s clear. Everybody run’. At the time, I never thought the towers would come down,” Bill says.

Eventually, everything inside the tower went eerily quiet and the rescuers realised they needed to leave. John went first to check it was safe before the others followed.

They had been outside for less than 30 seconds when the North Tower came crashing down, with John still inside.

Knowing John was gone, Bill curled into a ball as he was buried beneath the debris, believing he was going to die too.



At one point, he put a finger into his mouth to create an airway so he could breathe – and just as John had done shortly before, his thoughts immediately went to his family.

But Bill’s life was spared. When he realised he was still alive, he sprung into action to find the bodies of John and the people he was trapped with.

He says: “As soon as the buildings came down and I realised they were no longer there, I went searching for a chief and said, ‘We’ve got to go back and look for them’.



“I said, ‘I know where they’re at. They’re down here.’ Sure enough, months later, they were found there.”

Twelve members of Rescue 5 were working that day. Bill was the only one who came home.

He says: “When the North Tower was coming down and I was getting buried, the only people I said goodbye to were my wife and two boys.



“Since that day, that’s been my main focus in everything: prioritising my wife and two boys.”

But surviving when nearly 3,000 others didn’t brought a burden of its own.

Firefighters routinely witnessed death, Bill says, but dealt with it together back at the station before the next emergency demanded their attention.

September 11 was not something he could simply put behind him.

Bill says: “There was no forgetting it after losing all the guys I was working with. I knew I had to have counselling, so I sought it out.”



The first counsellor wasn’t right for him, but instead of abandoning therapy, Bill tried again and found someone he would continue seeing for four years.

He says: “It’s about living positively. I go to bed every single night and say, ‘Thank you for this day on Earth.’

“If I wake up tomorrow – and that’s a big if – then I’m going to make it a great day.”

There is, however, one question about his survival that has haunted him: why him?



Bill recalls: “I was once asked, ‘All the guys from your company died. Why do you think you lived?’ I said, ‘I guess God was just looking out for me’.

“He said to me, ‘God wasn’t looking out for all the other people who died?’

“That really hurt me. I didn’t know how to answer it.”

It was the widow of another firefighter killed on September 11 who eventually gave him an answer.



Bill says she told him: “Bill, you were chosen because you would continue to tell the story, carry on the events of that day and make sure we don’t forget.

“That’s so special. Don’t give it up. Keep talking about it, because we don’t want these people forgotten.”

Bill has since told his story “400 or 500 times”, including through educational talks and presentations at New York’s 9/11 Museum.

“I always talk about the guys from Rescue 5 and name them,” he says. “I think I’ve lived up to that promise to never forget the events of that day.”

He has also met the families of some of those he and John helped to save.



One woman told him her father had survived the attacks and lived for another decade.

Bill recalls: “She said, ‘We had 10 more years with my dad because of you.’ That’s a great feeling.”

That promise eventually brought Bill back to the D’Allara family.



He had met John’s wife Carol for lunch several years after the attacks and told her what had happened during her husband’s final moments, but John’s sons had been too young at the time.

When Bill finally sat down with John Jr and Nicolas for the documentary, they hadn’t spoken in 25 years.

At last, he told them how their father had helped force open the jammed door – and how his actions had helped save around 20 lives.

“I was apprehensive about whether what I had been doing all these years -talking about their dad in the way I did – was okay with them.

“I never wanted to mention anybody who had passed and then have somebody in the family become upset about something I had said.”



But the most important message was much simpler.

“The big thing is he was thinking about you until the very end,” Bill told them.

“That’s the most important thing I needed you to know.”

The meeting also allowed Bill to see what had become of the two little boys John had spoken about in the darkness.

“It was very emotional and gratifying. It was a weight lifted off my shoulders that I had relayed this message from their dad,” Bill says.



John Jr became a Marine reservist, while Nicolas followed his father into the police department and chose to work in the Bronx, where his dad had started his own career.

Carol even showed Bill John’s retired police badge – the same one her husband had worn and which can only be passed down through his children or grandchildren.

“Your dad would be proud of you,” Bill told them.

Carol, meanwhile, thanked the firefighter who had carried her husband’s memory for a quarter of a century.

“People say they’ll never forget and you’re one of the people who honoured that promise,” she told him.



For Bill, it was a moment decades in the making.

He says: “It was just wonderful. I feel like I got a lot off my chest and was able to finish the job I was supposed to do.”

As the 25th anniversary approaches, Bill is acutely aware that there is now a generation with no memory of September 11 at all.

He worries they are not being taught enough about the day that killed 2,977 people – including not only his colleagues and John, but his own uncle, who was a passenger on United Airlines Flight 93.

Bill says: “The biggest thing is how it started off as a normal day: beautiful blue skies and nice, clean, crisp air. So many people were going to work as if it were just another Tuesday.



“By the end of the day, so many families were affected and so many lives were lost.”

Both his sons went through school in New York, he says, yet their education about September 11 amounted to little more than an annual moment of silence.

He believes the attacks should be taught properly in schools so those born afterwards understand the human stories behind the numbers.

For Bill, that includes the extraordinary acts of courage he witnessed amid the horror.

He says: “Deep inside, it showed how good we all are as people. We have to think more positively – get that feeling deep inside out – and realise we’re all just people.



“We need to value life so much.”

And 25 years after meeting a stranger named John D’Allara in a pitch-black stairwell, Bill is still making sure the man who helped save so many lives is not forgotten.

9/11: Reunited is premiering from 9pm on Sunday 23rd August on National Geographic.
