World.title: French President Macron to host Saudi Crown Prince MBS in Paris for talks
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron is set to welcome Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) to Paris for a two-day state visit, opening with the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup before turning to talks on regional security and economic ties.

The visit begins Sunday evening as Macron hosts the crown prince at the esports tournament’s final in Paris — the first time the competition, spanning video games to chess, has been held outside Saudi Arabia.

Bilateral meetings and a business forum will follow on Monday, when Macron’s office said the two leaders will discuss “the main topics of regional importance, within a framework of close collaboration between France and her partners in the Gulf”.

What’s on the agenda

Officials expect discussion of energy routes that could bypass the Strait of Hormuz, including new pipelines, capacity upgrades and alternative port networks, alongside talks on the Iran conflict, Gaza-Israel and the wider situation in Palestine, and developments in Lebanon and Syria.

Several agreements on health, transport and energy are due to be signed on Monday. Macron’s adviser said finding a resolution to the US-Israel war on Iran, now in its sixth month, remains out of reach, noting “It’s difficult to see a way out.”

The visit is MBS’s third to Paris, following trips in 2022 and 2023, and builds on the Saudi-French Strategic Partnership Council launched during Macron’s state visit to Riyadh in December 2024.

The Paris trip is Prince Mohammed’s first outside the kingdom since Saudi Arabia signed a trilateral defence pact with Turkiye and Pakistan on August 7 — the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, known as the Mecca pact.



Signed by the prince as well as Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, the agreement commits all three states to treat an armed attack on any one of them as an attack on all three.

Analysts say the pact reflects Riyadh’s push to diversify its security partnerships beyond Washington.

The deal builds on a bilateral Saudi-Pakistan mutual defence agreement signed in 2025, and comes as Gulf states weigh how to reduce their reliance on US security guarantees amid the prolonged fallout from the Iran war.

France has been a long-standing weapons and defence supplier to Gulf states, and Saudi Arabia is positioning itself as a growing investor in the French economy.

The two leaders last met in April in Islamabad during talks between Tehran and Washington aimed at ending the Iran war, agreeing then to stay in “close contact” on de-escalation efforts.

Saudi Arabia is separately set to host Expo 2030 and the 2034 football World Cup, both likely to feature in Monday’s discussions.

World.title: Can Nigeria cash in on Iran war?
World.content:
Ekperikpe Ekpo says the US-Israel war on Iran has pushed Nigeria to expand its gas production.

The war in Iran has put global natural gas markets under strain, creating a potential opportunity for Nigeria to strengthen its position as a major gas supplier.

The country’s minister of state for petroleum resources, Ekperikpe Ekpo, discusses plans for the Nigeria-Morocco gas pipeline. He says Nigeria is seeking to attract investment, expand production and position its liquefied natural gas (LNG) for growing international demand, particularly in Europe.

But the opportunity comes as Nigerians continue to face high domestic cooking gas prices. Ekpo explains efforts to bring down liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices, move millions of households away from firewood, charcoal and kerosene, reduce gas flaring, and accelerate 20 gas projects towards final investment decisions before 2030.

World.title: Canada, US and tit-for-tat tariffs: How will they impact their economies?
World.content:
Both countries will suffer from the trade war, experts say, with steeper tariffs raising business costs and consumer prices.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced retaliatory tariffs that will “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar” after days of intense negotiations between the United States and Canada broke down.

The tit-for-tat response came after US President Donald Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports, disrupting the long history of stable relations between the two North American neighbours.

Trump first imposed tariffs on key imports from Canada early in his second term last year. The two countries have scuffled since with Trump periodically making new tariff threats.

So what prompted this latest escalation, and how will it impact the two Western economies?

How did talks break down?

In Ottawa on Saturday, Carney said the talks with the US broke down late the day before after Trump set conditions that were ultimately unacceptable.

“In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair and undermined the net benefits for Canada, and called into question the reliability of any deal,” Carney said, adding that these demands included curtailing Canada’s ability to forge new trade deals, in violation of its sovereignty.

“We’re the partner of choice in many respects for countries around the world, and the Americans wanted to restrict that. They had language that wanted to restrict that. Unacceptable.”

He added that US negotiators also made unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture”, referring to the French-speaking province in eastern Canada.



In a speech later in the day, Carney suggested that last-minute changes at the bargaining table had prompted him to recall his negotiators from Washington, DC, to Ottawa.

“In short, they asked too much, and they offered too little.”

Trump responded to Carney’s announcement by writing on his platform Truth Social: “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!” Trump has previously issued threats to annex Canada and make it the 51st US state.

The US president claimed Canada has also charged US farmers “massive amounts” of tariffs for years, adding, “No more!!!”

What Canadian products will be affected by the US tariffs?

The list of goods from Canada that will be affected is long, ranging from whisky to goose-down jackets and ice hockey equipment.

The 50 percent levy on roughly $20bn of Canadian goods covers more than 500 product categories, including:

Alcohol, such as beer, wine, liquor and cider. They will likely hit popular Canadian brands from Crown Royal whisky to Molson beer.

Dairy products from milk and cream to lactose syrup. Cheese, however, is not on the list even though Trump said a reason for the tariffs is Canada’s “discrimination” against US cheeses, The Washington Post reported.

Technology from smartphones to cameras, radar equipment and antennae

Athletic gear, notably equipment for hockey, one of two of Canada’s national sports. Other sports supplies targeted include those used in golf, at gyms and in swimming pools.

Wood products, including lumber, mouldings, plywood, furniture and fence components

Seasonal holiday products and gifts, including toys, clothing, Christmas decorations, jewellery, makeup and perfumes

The tariffs also apply to some products that were previously protected under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a trade pact signed during Trump’s first term, putting its future into question.

The new tariffs are being imposed in addition to pre-existing US tariffs on steel, lumber and cars.

What American products will be affected by Canadian tariffs?

Ottawa, meanwhile, said its retaliatory measures beginning on September 8 will target steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.

The Canadian government will release more details on the items to be targeted in the coming days, Carney said.

How will the trade war affect Canada’s economy?

Canada’s economy is expected to face a big blow from the tariffs, some experts said.

“Costs are going to go up. Prices are going to go up. Unemployment is going to go up as well,” Al Jazeera’s David Mercer said, reporting from Calgary, the largest city in the western province of Alberta.



“And it’s been warned that business owners – small [and] medium-sized businesses – some of those will have to declare bankruptcy,” he said.

Julian Karaguesian, a lecturer and trade expert at McGill University in Montreal, told Al Jazeera the tariffs would “effectively price hundreds of Canadian goods out of the US market”.

Key industries that are “important and politically influential”, including the alcohol, dairy and furniture industries, will take the biggest hit, Steven Okun, the CEO of APAC Advisors and a trade specialist, told Al Jazeera.

Still, with 5 percent of Canadian exports affected out of a $382bn market, he added, “it’s not a huge hit to the Canadian economy overall.”

At the same time, Mercer said, Carney is selling the trade war as an opportunity for Canada to strengthen its trade relations with other countries.

“He’s been around the world. He’s been talking to countries in Asia, in Europe, shoring up new trade relationships, wanting to diversify Canada’s economy and Canada’s trade relationships with other countries around the world just to get away from that dependency that Canada has traditionally had on the United States,” he said.

However, that’s a tall order. The majority of Canadian exports – a whopping 73 percent – are sold in the US, totalling $409bn last year, according to the financial data company Trading Economics.

The United Kingdom is next with 6 percent of Canadian exports going there while 4.4 percent of Canadian exports head to China, according to 2025 data cited by the firm, with the rest sold in various European and Asian markets.

How will the trade war affect the US economy?

Experts warned that steeper tariffs not only raise costs for businesses but they almost always trickle down to households in the form of higher prices, including in the US.

The Business Roundtable, a group of 200 chief executives of leading US corporations, warned that the new tariffs “risk raising costs for American businesses and families” and have called on both governments to resume negotiations.

Okun said the latest tariffs will be “politically painful” on both sides of the border.

Trump’s measures have neither increased trade for the US nor led to an increase in investment, as he said they would, and instead have caused inflation by raising prices, Okun explained.

Having a blanket tariff policy does not work, unlike targeted tariffs, he said.

“Targeted tariffs can work. They can work when you have a very specific issue like with China and their unfair trade practices and you target China … in a particular sector. Those can be effective,” he said.

“These writ-large tariffs are not effective. They’re hurting the United States, and it is very much hurting the Republican Party as they come up on these midterm elections” in November.

Diamond Isinger, who served as a special adviser to former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, said ultimately both countries will suffer from the trade war.

“It’s going to cause pain and challenge for Canadians and Americans alike in terms of the actions that, unfortunately, the US has taken as well as Canada’s retaliation. But ultimately, this was the way forward. This was the only realistic next step,” she said.

World.title: Iran’s government signals fuel price hike on eve of new US sanctions
World.content:
Prices for food and other items are already soaring, and there is a history of unrest, so any increase is being considered.

Tehran, Iran – The Iranian government is preparing the public for another increase in fuel prices as it attempts to buoy the country’s ailing economy.

With the United States’ siege of Iran’s seaports and the economic impact of the war continuing, the offer of heavily subsidised fuel to the country’s 93 million population is a burden that the government is struggling to afford.

The International Monetary Fund predicts that Iran’s gross domestic product (GDP) will contract by 5.4 percent in 2026.

Hiking the price of petrol in this oil-rich country has already sparked unrest before, including nationwide demonstrations in 2019. Such measures also preceded the January 2026 protests by several weeks.

So authorities are treading carefully, with a final decision expected over the coming weeks.

“I understand that we have many problems in society now. We are doing our best so the people are not afflicted, but the enemy is doing its absolute best so we won’t succeed,” President Masoud Pezeshkian said during a speech on Sunday morning, alluding to the six-month US-Israel war on Iran.

After US President Donald Trump threatened to target Iran with the “most crushing economic operation” ever undertaken against any country, the Iranian rial hit a new all-time low of 2 million rials per the US dollar in Tehran’s open market on Sunday afternoon.

On Friday, Pezeshkian noted that the price of fuel in Iran is considerably lower than in most countries in the world.

He said his administration pays 1.3 million rials (65 US cents at the current rate) per litre of petrol produced by refineries. The lowest price tier offered to the population is 15,000 rials (less than 1 cent) per litre (0.26 gallons).

Two other price categories for personal vehicle use – one at 30,000 rials (1.5 cents) per litre and the third at 50,000 rials (2.5 cents) – are also eating into the government’s finances.



Meanwhile, Iranians with imported, free-zone or newly registered vehicles are liable for the highest-price tier.

Still, there are limits to the amount of subsidised fuel Iranians can purchase, with each category having its own monthly quota, and sales are only allowed with a fuel card.

Pump stations have their own cards that offer some extra fuel at the highest-price category, but with a single-use limit of 25 litres in Tehran.

The quota for the cheapest category is 60 litres. From the start of the current calendar year in late March, authorities cut the quota for the second category from 100 to 70 litres. After two weeks of fighting between Iran and the US erupted again in July over the Strait of Hormuz, this allowance was cut again to 50 litres.

Iranians now consume roughly 135 million litres per day of fuel, with authorities saying earlier this month that production was at about 121 million litres per day.

To compensate for these financial losses, the government has attempted to increase refinery production, used petrochemical products, and reduced the quality of fuel by diluting it. Fuel imports have also stopped due to the war.

Three undesirable options

The government’s head of energy optimisation, Esmail Saghab-Esfahani, told state television last week that there are three options – each with their own complexities.

One option, he explained, is a first-come, first-served mechanism whereby prices would remain unchanged, but pump stations would simply shut down after running out of their allocated petrol.

Another is to offer all Iranians – including those without a vehicle – roughly 30 litres of fuel per month at the lowest price tier. Those who don’t drive could sell their monthly quota if they choose.

The third option is to liberalise the price of fuel for all, with the government reportedly considering a price of 872,000 rials (about 44 cents) per litre. But the consequence of this would be to create another huge inflationary bubble, with the massive increase in transport and logistics costs for businesses being passed on to consumers.

This price is closer to the refinery production price tag, and was almost implemented in a pilot programme in Kerman, the country’s largest province, in southeastern Iran.

Local authorities, reportedly in conjunction with the government, announced the new prices would be enforced in 204 pump stations across the province overnight into August 13. But the government cancelled the pilot scheme at the last minute, and contradicted local officials by saying they were not consulted on the move.



Nevertheless, the government has signalled that a considerable price increase is in the works.

On Friday, First Vice President Mohammad-Reza Aref said that the cheapest price tier with the 60-litre quota must remain in place. But the second quota could gradually fall, and prices should ultimately be liberalised transparently with proceeds directed toward vulnerable people.

“The government keeps talking about how fuel prices don’t match other countries, but it doesn’t like to talk about how salaries don’t even begin to match other places, or other expenses,” Mostafa, who earns 300 million rials ($150) a month working at a clothing shop in western Tehran, told Al Jazeera.

He explained that while the cost of driving to work in his 15-year-old Iranian-made vehicle does not factor heavily in his monthly calculations, housing, food and other runaway expenses are a major challenge after months of war, blockade and intensified US sanctions, as well as domestic mismanagement and state-imposed internet shutdowns.

Figures released by the Statistical Center of Iran in July reported that prices were 88 percent higher compared to the same month last year, with food inflation standing at over 128 percent.

A 55-year-old man working as a driver for multiple online ride-hailing services told Al Jazeera that conversations with passengers often turn into expressions of anger and frustration about the deteriorating living conditions in Iran.

“Everything will get more expensive a little while after fuel gets more expensive,” he said. “We’re already getting crushed by the prices we have today.”

World.title: PM Tarique Rahman’s trip stalled: What it means for Bangladesh-India ties
World.content:
New Delhi and Dhaka have not been able to move past the contentious question of Sheikh Hasina, the ousted Bangladeshi leader now living in exile in India.

New Delhi, India – Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s first trip to India has been put on hold, highlighting the strained ties between the two South Asian neighbours since the July 2024 student-led uprising that forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to flee the country.

Since coming to power in February, Rahman – the son of Hasina’s archrival, the late Khaleda Zia – has aimed to improve ties with India. But a press conference conducted by Hasina, who lives in India in exile, has riled Bangladesh.

Dhaka says that the August 5 press conference has “vitiated” the atmosphere, adding that “a propitious environment needs to be created for the visit” of Prime Minister Rahman.

For now, Rahman’s trip looks uncertain, as Bangladesh’s Foreign Ministry said officials from both countries have been engaged in talks for “several weeks” to work out a possible solution.

Here is everything you need to know about the latest diplomatic turbulence between the South Asian neighbours.

What’s up with Rahman’s India visit?

New Delhi had extended an invitation to Rahman for a stand-alone visit to India this month, ahead of next month’s scheduled BRICS summit. BRICS is a grouping of major emerging economies, currently chaired by India.

Since Rahman took office, there have been several exchanges between top ministers and diplomats from both sides. India appointed Dinesh Trivedi, a former minister and member of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), as its envoy to Dhaka in a rare political appointment to the key post.



Last Tuesday, Trivedi appealed to Rahman’s government, arguing that the Indian mission is not asking Dhaka “to forget the past”, in an apparent reference to Hasina’s exile in India. “Keep the past and sort out the differences of the past. But move on. Don’t get stagnant,” he added.

At a reception hosted by the Indian High Commission in Dhaka, Trivedi said that Modi wanted Rahman’s visit to be “memorable”.

But those plans for a visit were already derailed after Dhaka took offence to Hasina virtually addressing a presser at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club in New Delhi on August 5, marking two years of her ouster.

India clarified that it had nothing to do with the event, but to no avail.

What have both countries said?

Both capitals have been tight-lipped about Rahman’s visit. “I have nothing to say right now,” said India’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, responding to a question about Rahman’s visit.

Speaking at an event on Saturday, India’s Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said India and Bangladesh’s bilateral ties must meet the “test of mutual interest”.

“It has to work for them, it has to work for us,” he said.

“There has to be a reasonable degree of my recognising and respecting what is their interest, just as I expect them also to do so,” Jaishankar said.

Rahman’s foreign affairs adviser, Humayun Kabir, told a Bangladeshi news agency that there is “no rush” in Dhaka to facilitate the prime minister’s visit to India.

Kabir added that Dhaka is still ascertaining what kind of relationship India wants with the newly elected government in Bangladesh.

“The neighbouring country must properly understand the reality of Bangladesh’s July Mass Uprising, which took place through the sacrifices of more than 1,500 people,” he said, referring to India sitting on the request for Hasina’s extradition.

Earlier this month, New Delhi had said that it was considering Hasina’s extradition request based on the established procedure. Both countries have an extradition treaty, but with an exception for political cases.

What are the points of tension?

Bangladesh has made Hasina’s extradition a major issue. Hasina’s government was seen as especially close to India, and New Delhi’s backing of her authoritarian rule also angered Bangladeshis.

Dhaka has been seeking the extradition of Hasina, who was handed a death sentence in absentia in November 2025. Some analysts have accused New Delhi of using it as a diplomatic bargaining chip.



Bangladesh has expressed its displeasure with India for hosting Hasina and sees Hasina’s political speeches as an interference in its internal affairs. During the August 5 presser, Hasina said she would return to Bangladesh.

“We have requested Indian authorities to expeditiously act on our request to extradite Sheikh Hasina and other fugitive criminals,” the Bangladesh Foreign Ministry said in an X post on August 16.

“We reiterate that we will continue to pursue our ‘Bangladesh First’ policy to promote friendly bilateral relations with other countries, including our neighbours, on the basis of sovereign equality, national dignity, non-interference in each other’s internal affairs and mutual benefit.”

For New Delhi, Dhaka inching closer to Pakistan after decades of strained ties is a major diplomatic setback. India played a major role in the formation of Bangladesh from Pakistan in 1971.

Shakil Ahmed, an assistant professor of government and politics at Dhaka’s Jahangirnagar University, noted that domestic politics tends to influence foreign policy at times.

“Relations between India and Bangladesh are constrained by their domestic politics, especially in Dhaka,” he said.

“People in Bangladesh want that any relation with India should be based on self-respect and mutual interests,” he said, adding that Rahman’s government has been diversifying its friendships with foreign countries, including the US, China, and Pakistan.

“New Delhi saw Bangladesh as one of India’s foreign policy followers,” Ahmed said, noting that that is not the case anymore. “Hasina gave India a blank cheque in foreign relations, which is not happening anymore.”

India’s Hindu nationalist government’s push to fence the 4,096km-long (2,545-mile) border with Bangladesh has also strained ties. Anti-Bangladesh rhetoric by ruling party officials has further antagonised Dhaka.

India has been deporting what it calls undocumented Bangladeshi immigrants across its borders. Dhaka has accused New Delhi of pushing people extrajudicially into Bangladesh without diplomatic verification.

What’s ahead for India-Bangladesh ties?

Sanjay Bhardwaj, a professor of South Asian studies at the Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi, told Al Jazeera that Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Rahman is playing to the gallery by stalling his maiden India visit.

Hasina’s case is one of political persecution, said Bhardwaj, as her own government chased Rahman – who lived for the last 17 years in London, the United Kingdom, including all of Hasina’s years in power – with several criminal cases.

“India has been positive to cultivate and have a developmental partnership with Bangladesh, with no reluctance to develop the economic participation,” he added. “But Rahman is interested in politics and not thinking about the development of Bangladesh.”

Hasina’s extradition is a contentious issue, he said, adding that both capitals must move beyond this to maintain a productive bilateral relationship.

Sreeradha Datta, a professor specialising in South Asian studies at India’s OP Jindal Global University, said that both countries need to talk, since “there is no alternative”.



As neighbours, “they do not have a choice to disengage”, she said, adding that merely the passage of time will not repair the relations.

India is concerned about the Mecca defence pact, Datta told Al Jazeera, “But how can one have any control when there is no dialogue and engagement?”

“The initial warmth diluted in nationalistic noise on both sides,” Datta said, referring to initial interactions, including an Indian delegation led by Jaishankar visiting Dhaka last year for the funeral of Rahman’s mother, Khaleda Zia.

Datta argued that New Delhi needs to come to terms with a new reality that the government of Bangladesh may not share the same warmth as the one under Hasina did. “But that doesn’t matter,” she said. “These are neighbours, and a relationship based on objectives or interests is what will take it forward.”

World.title: Nordic nations ‘have lost confidence in Infantino’, demand FIFA reforms
World.content:
Six Nordic football associations have delivered a united blow to FIFA President Gianni Infantino, declaring they have lost confidence in his leadership while demanding sweeping governance reforms at world football’s governing body.

The six Nordic FIFA members – Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and the Faroe Islands – met in Helsinki and issued a rare joint statement on Sunday, backing calls for Infantino’s resignation from three major regional confederations.

They also supported demands for an independent investigation into his proposal to sell a stake in events like the World Cup to private equity investors, a plan that was quickly abandoned in the face of a global backlash.

“The six Nordic football associations have lost confidence in FIFA’s president and are concerned about the organisation’s governance and decision-making at the highest level,” they said in a statement.

“The Nordic football associations stand united with UEFA and support the measures that the organisation and its national member associations have jointly proposed.

“We expect FIFA to provide binding guarantees that the organisation’s governance or competitions will never again be opened up to private ownership.”

FIFA did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

On Friday, Denmark’s football association pledged to find a credible alternative to Infantino in March’s presidential election.

Infantino is under pressure from three confederations to resign: UEFA, the AFC and CONCACAF.

The sport’s regional powerhouses in Europe, Asia, and North and Central America and the Caribbean have also discussed a potential vote of no confidence against the FIFA chief.



“We also support the demand made by AFC, CONCACAF and UEFA that a fully independent external investigation into the events surrounding the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal be established,” the Nordic associations added.

“We also call on FIFA to initiate a comprehensive and independent review of its governance framework to determine whether it ensures the independence, checks and balances, transparency and accountability that were intended when FIFA adopted its reform programme in 2016.”

Infantino, who is seeking a fourth term until 2031 in next year’s election, is in the Dominican Republic this weekend, where he has met with officials of the Caribbean Football Union (CFU).

CONCACAF President Victor Montagliani had asked Infantino to stay away from a youth football tournament in the country, saying his presence would overshadow the event.

“This meeting of the presidents of CFU takes place in the environment of [an] under-14 youth tournament in the region, which actually is one of those tournaments that can take place thanks to the FIFA Forward programme,” Infantino said.

“So even more so a reason to be proud to be here and happy as well because it’s important to engage, to have a dialogue, to express views and opinions.”

World.title: Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has said Canada wants "the benefits of being a State, without being one" after trade talks between the two countries collapsed late on Friday.

In his first comments since negotiations broke down, triggering new 50% US tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, Trump also said American farmers had been charged "massive amounts of Tariffs" for years.

It comes after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the fresh tariffs a "miscalculation" designed to "hurt and divide us".

Carney confirmed he would match Trump's tariffs "dollar-for-dollar" from 8 September, including levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. The US and Canada are now in a trade "war", he said.

"They asked too much and they offered too little," Carney said on Saturday. "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he added.

Trump's latest comments echo his repeated references to making Canada the "51st state" of America since returning to office, sparking frustration among its leaders and residents.

The collapse of the trade talks upended a deeply integrated trading relationship, with no clear path to resolution.

"We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said.

Both countries were optimistic of a deal earlier in the week, but talks fell apart after both sides accused the other of making last-minute changes.

The new 50% US tariffs will apply to a range of Canadian goods, in addition to existing US tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.

They are limited in scope, covering about $20bn (Â£15bn; C$28bn) of Canadian imports, or about 5% in total, including wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.

The prime minister said Canada was retaliating "reluctantly" to protect its interests. Details of the counter-measures will be released in the coming days, he said.

World.title: Zelensky should be asked what he knew about government corruption, sacked minister tells BBC
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky should be asked questions about corruption in his government, his sacked defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has told the BBC.

Fedorov, a popular minister who modernised the military and pioneered drone warfare, was fired last month after reportedly falling out with the head of Ukraine's armed forces.

He told the BBC a money laundering investigation announced last week meant Zelensky should be asked about his awareness of potential corruption in his inner circle.

But he said he had not himself seen the president engage in any corrupt activity.

"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity", Federov said.

The former minister also repeated his appeal for elections to be held in Ukraine, days after releasing a video where he called for a wartime vote.

"Democracy should not be the hostage of Putin", he said - but stopped short of declaring his own political ambitions.

There were angry protests over Fedorov's sacking but his support dwindled and demonstrations ended on Wednesday, after his replacement was confirmed. His call for a vote has been widely rejected.

Asked whether he missed his old job, the 35-year-old replied "No", citing the relentless stress of managing Ukraine's war with Russia while transforming its defence ministry.

Ukraine has been under martial law since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, meaning elections are suspended. Zelensky's five-year presidential term ended in May 2024.

But Fedorov said it was his "moral right" to start the conversation about elections.

"We should not be afraid of discussing it. That's what democracy is all about. If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for?"

If elections were never held, he said, "then we are no longer a democracy".

World.title: DR Congo and M23 rebels agree roadmap for peace talks
World.content:
The Democratic Republic of Congo government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group have agreed a roadmap for peace talks.

In a joint statement after five days of talks in Switzerland, they said they had pledged to "pursue negotiations towards comprehensive peace and conflict resolution" and set up a mechanism to monitor the ceasefire.

The roadmap sets out a timeline for talks under a US-brokered peace framework which they signed in 2025 - only for fighting to then continue in eastern DR Congo, which has been engulfed in conflict for decades.

But disagreements remain over issues including sanctions against M23, the release of detainees and the timing of political reforms.

The latest negotiations were attended by M23, the government of DR Congo, Qatar, the US, the Republic of Togo, the African Union Commission and host Switzerland.

"The parties agreed to establish a mechanism tasked with reviewing progress and addressing challenges in implementation of obligations and commitments under the Doha Framework Agreement," the statement added, referring to the 2025 deal.

They developed "sequenced steps and timelines" while also committing to "flexibility and creativity", the statement said.

They also agreed to implement a mechanism to monitor ceasefire violations. Its secretariat has been established and the first verification mission is due to take place on Monday in Minembwe, an area of South Kivu affected by fighting.

Fighting has continued in North and South Kivu despite repeated ceasefire commitments, with the government and M23 accusing each other of violations.

World.title: Dozens of co-ordinated arson attacks hit southern Thailand
World.content:
More than 50 co-ordinated arson and incendiary attacks "aimed at creating unrest" have been carried out across Thailand's insurgency-hit south, the Thai military has said.

At least two people were injured, with a local government office building, a convenience store, and a stolen vehicle among the targets set on fire.

The incidents took place across the country's southern border provinces between 20:00 local time (13:00 GMT) and midnight on Saturday, the military's Internal Security Operations Command said in a statement.

Most were reported in Narathiwat province, with others occurring in neighbouring Yala and Pattani.

According to the Bangkok Post, two women were injured when a bomb exploded in Muang district in Narathiwat province.

Telecommunication towers were set on fire in several locations, and security officials warned residents not to touch suspicious objects.

Authorities imposed an overnight curfew in the Narathiwat province that was lifted on Sunday morning. No further attacks had been reported on Sunday.

World.title: France links rise in drownings to heatwaves
World.content:
France has seen 301 drownings since 19 June, a government minister has said, linking the sharp rise in deaths compared to last year to the prolonged heatwaves.

Sports and Youth Minister Marina Ferrari told France Inter radio the number of deaths - a 14% hike on 2025 - was a "tragic toll".

France, Spain and Italy have been hit by heatwaves, which have triggered massive wildfires that scorched thousands of hectares of land.

Ferrari said people have been taking risks by going into the water, adding: "Many deadly accidents have occurred in areas that are not authorised or supervised for swimming."

She said a number of the drownings were recorded in "open water, in canals for example".

Ferrari said the government was working with regional authorities "to improve swimming areas and make things safer".

Speaking on Friday, she added that "many drownings, particularly among the elderly, occurred in individual pools".

The minister said that sudden immersion in colder water on a hot day could cause shock, and in some cases "people can also exceed their physical capabilities".

In June, Ferrari warned that too many people were trying to cool off in rivers and canals without necessarily taking the risks into account.

Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world - but particularly in Europe.

It is the fastest warming content, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service., external

World.title: Thousands struggling without power in Indiana 12 days after severe storms
World.content:
Nearly two weeks after a damaging storm struck her town in Indiana, Terry Dubois is one of tens of thousands of people still without power.

The 77-year-old has been relying on friends to bring her non-perishable food to eat.

Her son brought her a power bank so she can charge her phone and keep in touch with the outside world.

Thankfully, the summer heat hasn't been too punishing, Dubois said, meaning she has not missed her air conditioning too much.

"I've never seen a storm like that in my entire life. Never, never," she tells the BBC.

"It was like a sheer wall of wind," she recalls.

A wave of sudden, severe storms brought flooding and tornadoes to the US Midwest on 11 August, including to Chicago and Indiana, where seven people were killed.

The former industrial town of Gary, which runs along the southern shore of Lake Michigan, was hit particularly hard. Wind gusts peaked at 99mph (159kmh), according to the National Weather Service.

The worst of the storm only lasted five to 10 minutes, but the impacts are lingering 12 days later.

World.title: The hotel booking mix-up that could free mushroom murderer
World.content:
Last July, hundreds descended on Australia's Gippsland region from around the country for the most exciting event on the annual table tennis calendar.

But as elite players vied for medals at the national championships, one of the biggest criminal cases in the nation's history - that of mushroom murderer Erin Patterson - was unfolding just a few kilometres away.

This tournament inadvertently became part of a perfect storm which the triple killer's lawyers are now arguing "fatally undermined" the fairness of her trial.

The jury which condemned Patterson to prison were supposed to be isolated - sheltered from the frenzy surrounding the case while they deliberated.

But accommodation shortages in the region, exacerbated by the table tennis competition, meant they shared a hotel with members of the prosecution, a key police witness, and journalists.

Now Patterson's legal team is trying to overturn her convictions on appeal.

"The only proper remedy is... the order for a re-trial," Patterson's barrister Richard Edney said.

World.title: Kejelcha breaks men's half marathon world record by 29 seconds
World.content:
Ethiopia's Yomif Kejelcha has broken the men's half marathon world record, winning a World Athletics road race in Buenos Aires on Sunday in 56 minutes 51 seconds.

The 29-year-old previously held the record with a time of 57:30, set in Valencia in October 2024, but lost that to Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo in March.

Kiplimo ran 57:20 in Lisbon earlier this year but Kejelcha has now knocked 29 seconds off that time to regain the record, subject to official ratification.

The world track silver medallist in the 10,000m also holds the world record for a men's 10,000m road race.

He also became one of the first men to run a sub-two hour marathon in record-eligible conditions earlier this year when finishing second behind Kenya's Sebastian Sawe in the London Marathon.

Sawe won the record-breaking race in 1:59:30, beating Kejelcha by just 11 seconds.

World.title: Famadewa, Ribadu and a 90-day security plan: Unpacking Onanuga’s release, By Yushau A Shuaib
World.content:
The logical question the ninety‑day committee must answer before drafting a single page is simple: What is the relationship between its new mandate and the frameworks that already exist? Is the new Strategic Defence Operations Plan intended to replace NACTEST, the NCMD, and the NCTC Strategic Plan? Will it sit alongside them? Is it a military‑specific operational layer beneath the broader national security architecture? If so, how will coordination be ensured?

When the Presidential Spokesman, Bayo Onanuga, announced that President Bola Tinubu had constituted an eleven‑man committee to develop a National Threat Assessment and a Strategic Defence Operations Plan within ninety days, several things struck me about this – with about four months to the next general elections, even before I reached the substance of the directive.

The first was a detail so small that it might ordinarily escape notice. The release identified Major General Adeyinka A Famadewa, the President’s Special Adviser on Homeland Security, being tasked to coordinate the committee and provide secretariat support. His name appeared without the designation Rtd. — retired — after his military rank. In routine communication, such an omission may be a harmless editorial slip. But in security communication, precision is not a luxury; it is a discipline.

The substance of the directive, however, is consequential. The President has mandated the committee to produce the plan that will establish medium‑term operational priorities by identifying force requirements, capability gaps, and equipment needs across all theatres.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The committee’s membership is composed of named individuals, not offices — a significant distinction. It includes the National Security Adviser, Malam Nuhu Ribadu; the Minister of Defence, General Christopher Musa; the Minister of State for Defence, Alhaji Bello Muhammad Matawalle; the Chief of Defence Staff, General Olufemi Oluyede; the service chiefs; and the heads of the State Security Service and National Intelligence Agency. Naming individuals, rather than offices, removes the flexibility of substitution and attaches personal accountability to the mandate. That means the meeting with not be by representation or delegation.

Yet the composition raises legitimate questions that the release did not address. The Inspector General of Police and the Chief of Defence Intelligence are absent. So are the heads of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps and the Nigeria Immigration Service. Whether these omissions reflect a deliberate architectural choice or an oversight is unclear. But in a country where internal security, public order, and counter‑insurgency rely heavily on policing and civil defence structures, their absence is not a trivial matter.

The release cited a single operational event — the rescue of pupils and teachers abducted in Oriire Local Government Area of Oyo State — as justification for the new initiative. The rescue was indeed commendable. But anchoring a national‑level defence planning directive on one successful southern operation inadvertently reinforces the asymmetry in how security successes across Nigeria’s regions are framed. Comparable and often larger rescue operations in the North‑East and North‑West — from freeing abducted students to reclaiming communities from insurgents — have received far less national attention.

Nigeria is not a country that lacks security strategy documents. If anything, it has produced them in abundance. The ninety‑day mandate would benefit from an honest reckoning with what already exists — and what became of it.

Onanuga’s release contains a paragraph that deserves particular attention. It states that once approved, the proposed plan “would serve as the principal framework for coordinating military and defence operations over the medium term” and would guide a multi‑year defence expenditure and procurement plan… The emphasis on military and defence operations and spending — rather than national security in the broader sense — is telling.

In 2013, under President Goodluck Jonathan, Nigeria launched a comprehensive national security architecture built on three interconnected documents: the National Counter Terrorism Strategy (NACTEST), the National Security Strategy (NSS) and the National Cybersecurity Policy and Strategy.

NACTEST, initiated by NSA Colonel Sambo Dasuki (Rtd), rested on five pillars — Forestall, Secure, Identify, Prepare, and Implement — and mandated periodic reviews every five to ten years.

Under President Muhammadu Buhari, the Office of the National Security Adviser, led by Major General Babagana Monguno (Rtd), revised the framework of NACTEST and launched the National Crisis Management Doctrine (NCMD) in 2022. The NCMD translated broad policy directives into concrete crisis protocols, establishing standardised command structures, strategic communication channels, and escalation pathways for coordinated national response.

Under the current administration, the Office of the National Security Adviser unveiled the NCTC Strategic Plan 2025–2030, a five‑year roadmap for preventing and countering violent extremism built on intelligence fusion, inter‑agency collaboration, operational capacity building, and strategic communications. It was unveiled in November 2025 by Senate President Godswill Akpabio on behalf of President Tinubu, while NCTC Cordinator Major General Adamu Garba Laka represented Ribadu at the occasion.

The logical question the ninety‑day committee must answer before drafting a single page is simple: What is the relationship between its new mandate and the frameworks that already exist? Is the new Strategic Defence Operations Plan intended to replace NACTEST, the NCMD, and the NCTC Strategic Plan? Will it sit alongside them? Is it a military‑specific operational layer beneath the broader national security architecture? If so, how will coordination be ensured?

Onanuga’s release contains a paragraph that deserves particular attention. It states that once approved, the proposed plan “would serve as the principal framework for coordinating military and defence operations over the medium term” and would guide a multi‑year defence expenditure and procurement plan.

The emphasis on military and defence operations and spending — rather than national security in the broader sense — is telling. It may align with the committee’s composition, which is heavily weighted towards the armed services and intelligence agencies, and with the choice of a retired Major General Famadewa as coordinator, rather than the NSA whose remit covers the entire national security spectrum.

A ninety‑day planning exercise can produce a credible framework, but it must be backed by a realistic, legislatively supported multi‑year funding commitment. It should not demand excessive new spending, especially at a time when the country continues to borrow heavily for major capital projects.

Ribadu’s background is in civilian law enforcement, and he retired as an Assistant Inspector General of Police following his distinguished career at the EFCC and in politics. His placement as a member rather than coordinator reflects a committee architecture that is primarily military in orientation. Whether this orientation is appropriate for Nigeria’s diverse security challenges — from economic crimes and banditry to coastal piracy and electoral violence — is a legitimate question for scholars and policymakers.

The most consequential paragraph in the release is the one that received the least attention. It notes that the proposed framework will guide multi‑year defence expenditure, ensuring resources are directed toward agreed operational priorities. That is funding — and funding is where seriousness is ultimately tested.

Nigeria has a long history of producing sophisticated security strategy documents that were quietly shelved once the budget cycle arrived and political priorities shifted. The question now is whether the new plan will emphasise expenditure more than operational efficiency — and whether it will avoid becoming another well‑written document without practical impact.

A ninety‑day planning exercise can produce a credible framework, but it must be backed by a realistic, legislatively supported multi‑year funding commitment. It should not demand excessive new spending, especially at a time when the country continues to borrow heavily for major capital projects.

In the concluding paragraph of the release, the President tasked not individual officers but the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (OSGF) and the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) to give immediate effect to the directive. Their compliance — and the quality of output from the committee’s named members — will define the next ninety days.

With the general election approaching, the ninety days will tell us much, while the budget will tell us the rest.

Yushau A. Shuaib is the author of MNI Versus MNIPR in NIPSS- Tackling institutional Bullying. Email: [email protected]

World.title: How honour connected me with Mr Tony Elumelu, By Ayo Akerele
World.content:
When honour paves the way, doors automatically swing open before you. Throughout my life, countless high-level doors have opened simply because I chose to honour the individuals occupying those positions of influence. For many people today, spiritual opposition is not the root cause of their ongoing stagnation; rather, it is their evident disregard for respecting and honouring others, whether young or old, rich or poor.

Years ago, while residing in Europe, I reached a point where I felt a strong desire to return home to Nigeria. At the time, I was feeling somewhat exhausted and disillusioned with life abroad. Prior to moving to Europe, I had been balancing active ministry work in South Africa with my professional career as an engineer. While in Europe, I pursued an MBA while concurrently serving in ministry with the Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG). Yet, despite my active involvement in both spheres, a distinct sense of weariness set in. After seeking divine direction through prayer, I felt a clear spiritual redirection calling me back to my home country.

However, returning required a viable and sustainable source of income. I was in my thirties, still a young professional, and I knew I could not afford to return to Nigeria without a clear plan, only to spend months hunting for employment. That was when an ambitious idea struck me: Why not reach out directly to Mr Tony Elumelu, pitch my value proposition, and express my explicit interest in working for him?

At that stage in my career, I had already earned an MBA, alongside two bachelors degrees, complemented by more than seven years of hands-on professional experience spanning banking, investment, and the mining sector. Furthermore, I had previously met Mr Elumelu in the year 2000, while he was serving as the Managing Director of Standard Trust Bank (STB). He had personally interviewed me in Lagos back then, though he did not extend a job offer to me at that time. Reflecting on this history, I strategised my approach and, through what felt like a miraculous turn of events, managed to secure his private email address.

Without hesitation, I drafted a comprehensive letter to Mr Elumelu, earnestly asking for an opportunity to transition back to Nigeria under his leadership. I made a conscious effort to saturate that letter with immense respect, reverence, and honour. To my absolute astonishment, in under 24 hours, I received a personal reply from him, inviting me to meet him at the iconic Dorchester Hotel in London. I was dazed; my strategy had worked.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Upon my arrival at the Dorchester Hotel, he instructed me to come directly upstairs to his private suite. I could hardly believe this was happening. I practically sprinted up the escalators to reach his room on the third or fourth floor. When I knocked, he opened the door and casually walked back to sit on the edge of the bed. Inside the room, I met three of his top executive team members, two gentlemen and a lady, who had gathered to discuss critical business operations.

Mr Elumelu looked at me, smiled, and offered a few lighthearted remarks, admitting he was genuinely astonished by the sheer audacity it took for me to write directly to him. I humbly defended my strategy, further cementing my respect in his heart.

He then inquired about my depth of experience in the mining industry, followed by a concise discussion regarding my background in banking. To make a long story short, he hired me right there at the Dorchester as an expatriate staff member.

I felt as though I was walking in the third heaven. He told one of his directors to give me some money. I was given £400. You don’t know what £400 was at that time. My monthly rent was £300. Overjoyed, I rushed downstairs, immediately called my wife to share the incredible news, and, as the saying goes, the rest is history. Although subsequent developments later led to a change of plans that required me to remain in Europe, that singular moment changed my perspective forever.

If you were to read the original letter I addressed to Mr Elumelu over two decades ago, you would be amazed by its posture. I honoured his leadership to the highest degree. I carefully aligned his remarkable global achievements and extraordinary banking success with my own professional competencies and international exposure, presenting the narrative in a manner that resonated deeply with him.

This experience holds profound life lessons for all of us. Today, I frequently observe young individuals displaying a form of boldness and audacity that is completely devoid of honour, seemingly oblivious to the immense professional and relational costs of such arrogance. Similarly, certain older individuals also make the grave mistake of withholding respect from others. Social media has become the graveyard of honour for this generation.

In the African context specifically, have you ever wondered why many individuals hesitate to disclose their true ages during birthday celebrations? It stems from a societal tendency to measure respect strictly through the narrow lenses of age, race, financial status, and corporate position.

If you were to read the original letter I addressed to Mr Elumelu over two decades ago, you would be amazed by its posture. I honoured his leadership to the highest degree. I carefully aligned his remarkable global achievements and extraordinary banking success with my own professional competencies and international exposure, presenting the narrative in a manner that resonated deeply with him. Ultimately, it was not merely my technical credentials or my résumé that opened that prestigious door, it was the principle of honour. Honour possesses the extraordinary ability to accomplish for you in a single day what your skills, knowledge, and hard-fought qualifications might struggle to achieve over twenty years.

On numerous occasions, relative strangers have boldly sent direct messages to my inbox, addressing me casually by my first name. I usually laugh and refrain from responding altogether. As a standard of propriety, one should not address unfamiliar individuals by their first names without prior rapport. Even when an acquaintance exists, professional and social titles serve as vital symbols of respect.

Utilising titles such as Madam, Mister, Mrs, Doctor, or Pastor acknowledges an individual’s sacrifices, societal contributions, personal labour, and long-standing commitments. The privilege of using a person’s first name ought to be reserved strictly for contexts involving mutual consent and established familiarity.

Contrary to popular belief, modern Western culture does not negate this fundamental principle. Having lived and worked in both Europe and North America for several decades, I can confidently state that while first-name familiarity is integrated into certain corporate environments, it is by no means universal across all societal domains. In Western societies, professionals regularly address physicians by their professional designations, just as they do with public officials, referring to them formally as Senator James, President Smith, or Governor Andrew.

Imagine if I had initiated my letter to a corporate titan like Mr Elumelu by writing, “Hi Tony, how are you doing?” That letter would have been discarded immediately. It is essential for the younger generation to move past casual, dismissive tendencies, recognise the boundaries of proper conduct, and rebuild their personal values upon the solid pillars of honour.

To this day, I make it a priority to honour a vast network of people, including friends, ministers, spiritual fathers, and missionaries, by quietly supporting their ministries, standing faithfully by them during moments of crisis, and never exploiting their personal vulnerabilities or moments of weakness against them. Consequently, whenever I reach out to them for guidance or assistance, they respond with overwhelming generosity.

For me personally, the prerogative to address me solely by my first name belongs exclusively to my biological parents, my wife, a select group of childhood friends, and my spiritual parents, and even among them, many still choose to speak with elevated respect.

Furthermore, when interacting with married women, addressing them as Madam reflects proper etiquette. In traditional African culture, it is common practice to show deference to married women by identifying them through their children’s names, such as Mama John or Mama Kunle.

The Enduring Impact of Walking in Honour

A highly revered senior spiritual father in the Nigerian church once asked me to stop addressing him as “Daddy.” Out of deep respect for his stature, I respectfully declined his request. When he pressed the issue further, I still could not bring myself to abandon that posture of deference. To maintain harmony without compromising my values, I adopted a balanced approach in my correspondence, structuring my letters and messages with: “Dear Sir” or “Hello Sir,” proceeding with the core message, and consistently concluding with: “Sir, please convey my warmest regards to Mummy.”

Despite his initial preference, he could not prevent me from extending profound honour to his beloved wife of over forty years by calling her “Mummy.” They ultimately opened their hearts and their home to my family and I. That is the undeniable power of intentional honour.

To this day, I make it a priority to honour a vast network of people, including friends, ministers, spiritual fathers, and missionaries, by quietly supporting their ministries, standing faithfully by them during moments of crisis, and never exploiting their personal vulnerabilities or moments of weakness against them. Consequently, whenever I reach out to them for guidance or assistance, they respond with overwhelming generosity.

For instance, when I recently required the direct contact information of a prominent worship leader in Nigeria, I approached this same spiritual father. Within 24 hours, he personally facilitated the introduction and provided me with the private mobile number I needed.

That is precisely what honour achieves. When honour paves the way, doors automatically swing open before you. Throughout my life, countless high-level doors have opened simply because I chose to honour the individuals occupying those positions of influence. For many people today, spiritual opposition is not the root cause of their ongoing stagnation; rather, it is their evident disregard for respecting and honouring others, whether young or old, rich or poor. When you walk in genuine honour, your path in life becomes remarkably smooth.

Ayo Akerele is the senior pastor of Rhema Assembly and the founder of the Voice of the Watchmen Ministries in Ontario, Canada. He can be reached through [email protected]. World.title: From employee to industry authority (2), By Yemi Adetayo
World.content:
Don’t spend your entire career simply climbing the corporate ladder, while remaining unknown outside your office. Don’t retire with decades of experience that nobody can benefit from because you never documented, taught or shared it. Don’t allow your knowledge to disappear when your employment ends. Build something bigger than your job. Build expertise. Build relationships. Build credibility. Build a body of knowledge. Build a reputation for solving problems. Build people. Build platforms. Build influence. And above all, build a legacy.

“The future depends on what you do today.” — Mahatma Gandhi

There is a significant difference between having a job and building a professional legacy. To become an employee, you may need the requisite certification, skills, knowledge, experience and the right attitude. You apply for a position, go through the recruitment process, get hired and begin your career. You learn the job, meet expectations, receive your salary and hopefully progress through the ranks.

Becoming an industry authority requires much more. An employee is paid to perform a role. An authority becomes a reference point. An employee occupies a position; an authority occupies a place of influence. An employee contributes to an organisation; an authority contributes to the industry. When people have questions, they seek the authority. When organisations need expertise, they call the authority. When emerging professionals need direction, they look up to the authority.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The good news is that industry authority is not reserved for a privileged few. Anyone can become an authority if they are willing to know what to do and do what it takes. The journey begins with a decision.

1. Get a career vision. That is where success begins.

Before you become an industry authority, you must first see yourself becoming one. Vision is one of the most important requirements for meaningful success in career and life. Without vision, you may spend years working hard without knowing what you are ultimately building. You can have a job without having a vision. You can receive a salary without having a destination. You can be busy every day and still be moving nowhere significant.

This is why you must ask yourself a deeper question: Beyond my current job title, who do I want to become in this industry? Do you want to become the person people consult? The person organisations invite to speak? The professional whose opinions shape conversations? The expert who trains others? The author whose books influence the next generation? The consultant who solves difficult industry problems? You must see it before you can systematically build it.

Your current job should not be the boundary of your professional ambition. It should be the laboratory in which you develop the expertise, experience and credibility required for the larger contribution you intend to make. Don’t merely work for a company. Build yourself while working for the company.

2. Join the Right Professional Association

There are professional associations in every field. Find the ones relevant to your profession and become a member. But understand this: membership alone does not make you influential. Some professionals join associations, pay annual dues, attend an occasional meeting, collect certificates and disappear until renewal time. That is membership. Authority requires active participation.

Join a committee. Volunteer for a project. Contribute an idea. Attend conferences. Network with professionals outside your immediate organisation. Ask questions. Share your expertise. Offer to help. Volunteer to speak when opportunities arise. There is tremendous professional capital hidden in service.

When you serve, people get to know you. When you contribute, people discover your competence. When you consistently add value, people begin to trust you. And when trust and competence meet consistently over time, you influence becomes visible.

Greatness is often hidden in the place of service. That committee you are avoiding may introduce you to people who will open doors you never knew existed. That professional conference where you volunteer may become the platform from which your expertise is discovered. Don’t just join a professional body, become active, participate. Beyond participation, contribute. And don’t stop there, take the lead.

3. Become a Specialist

You cannot become an industry authority by being a professional who knows a little about everything but is known for nothing. Develop an area of specialisation.

Find the problems your industry is struggling with and become deeply knowledgeable about solving some of them. Read widely. Take courses. Attend conferences. Study emerging trends. Research your field. Follow industry developments. Learn from experts. Experiment. Reflect on your experiences. Most importantly, turn experience into expertise.

You have encountered situations that somebody else is encountering for the first time. You have made mistakes that could save someone years of frustration. You have discovered approaches that work. You have seen what fails. Document these lessons. Your experience becomes more valuable when you can convert it into knowledge that helps other people perform better.

4. Use Social Media as a Professional Platform

You no longer need to own a television station, newspaper or publishing company before your ideas can reach thousands of people. With smart phone, you can now reach the world. You can publish from your phone.

Platforms such as LinkedIn, Facebook and other digital channels have created unprecedented opportunities for professionals to share knowledge, experiences, insights and perspectives. Use them wisely and adequately.

Write about what you know. Explain difficult concepts. Share lessons from your career. Comment intelligently on industry developments. Tell stories about challenges you have overcome. Share practical solutions. Someone somewhere may be struggling with the very problem whose solution you have already mastered. Your experience could become somebody else’s breakthrough.

Do not underestimate the power of a thoughtful article, a useful LinkedIn post, a short video or a well-articulated professional opinion. You may think nobody is reading. Keep writing. Keep sharing. Keep adding value. Influence often begins quietly before it becomes visible.

5. Become a Mentor

One of the clearest signs that you are growing professionally is your willingness to help others grow. There are people around you who need what you know. At work, someone may need guidance. A younger professional may need career direction. A student may need someone to help them see possibilities beyond their current circumstances. Someone on social media may need the lesson you learnt through years of experience.

Make yourself available. And don’t only tell people about your successes. Tell them about your failures too.Your victories can inspire people, while your failures will instruct them. Tell them about the opportunities you missed. Tell them about the decisions you got wrong. Tell them about the lessons you learnt the hard way. Tell them what you wish someone had told you when you were starting.

There is power in saying: I have been there. I made that mistake. Here is what I learnt. Mentoring is not only about transferring knowledge. It is about transferring perspective too. Sometimes, the greatest evidence of your professional growth is not how many people know your name, but how many lives are better because you were available.

6. Write. Teach. Publish.

If you want to become a major influence in your industry, develop the discipline of sharing knowledge publicly. Write articles. Start a professional blog. Contribute to industry publications. Write research papers. Develop training materials. Speak at conferences. Teach courses. Eventually, write a book.

Writing forces you to organise your thinking. Teaching forces you to understand your subject deeply. Publishing creates a record of your ideas. A book can travel where you cannot. An article can remain accessible long after a presentation is forgotten. A recorded lecture can educate people you may never meet.

Every time you write something useful, you are leaving a piece of your professional thinking in the world. Don’t die with your knowledge inside you. Package it. Share it. Teach it. Publish it. Let your knowledge outlive your job title.

7. Build Influence Before You Need It

One of the greatest mistakes professionals make is waiting until they need visibility before they start building it. They wait until they want a promotion before developing relationships. Don’t wait. Build your professional reputation now.

Your employer gives you a platform to gain experience. Your profession gives you a platform to build expertise. Professional associations give you opportunities to serve. Social media gives you a platform to communicate. Mentoring gives you an opportunity to multiply your knowledge. Use all of them. Your goal is beyond just becoming famous. Your goal is to become valuable, credible and trusted.

Visibility without value is noise. But when visibility is built on competence, character, contribution and consistency, it becomes influence.

The Industry Is Waiting for You

Don’t spend your entire career simply climbing the corporate ladder, while remaining unknown outside your office. Don’t retire with decades of experience that nobody can benefit from because you never documented, taught or shared it. Don’t allow your knowledge to disappear when your employment ends. Build something bigger than your job. Build expertise. Build relationships. Build credibility. Build a body of knowledge. Build a reputation for solving problems. Build people. Build platforms. Build influence. And above all, build a legacy.

The world does not merely need more employees. Every industry needs professionals who are willing to think, innovate, teach, serve, solve problems and raise the standard of practice.

Your industry is beckoning. Will you make yourself available? Don’t just be an employee. Become an industry influence.

“If your actions inspire others to dream more, learn more, do more and become more, you are a leader.” — John Quincy Adams
