World.title: Stray animal highway horror
World.content:
The mangled Mitsubishi Pajero involved in the August 15 crash on the May Pen to Williamsfield leg of Highway 2000.

TOLL GATE, Clarendon — A night of T20 cricket enjoyment at Sabina Park in Kingston just over a week ago almost ended in death for three people when the sport utility vehicle in which they were travelling back to Mandeville crashed into a cow that had wandered onto the May Pen to Williamsfield leg of Highway 2000 in pitch darkness.

Hopeton McCatty, the driver and owner of the Mitsubishi Pajero; his friend Wensworth Skeffery, a former Opposition senator; and Skeffery’s 24-year-old daughter were not injured, but the cow died in the August 15 collision that revived fears of the danger posed to life by stray animals on the high-speed road.

“We took my friend’s daughter to cricket for the first time and she enjoyed it; a very good game of cricket, a fantastic crowd. We left Sabina Park and went downtown then joined the toll road at Portmore,” McCatty told the Jamaica Observer.

“We were talking about the experience of interacting with people and how to be humble. We were cruising along. We came through the tolls at Portmore, Vineyards, and May Pen. We were approaching the last one at Toll Gate driving at about 103 kilometres per hour… I had on the high beam, because the road was dark. We were in the left lane and while talking Skeffery said ‘Cow!’ ” McCatty related.

“I spotted this animal coming onto the road, so I braked and swerved to the right and we really thought we had missed it, but the cow kept coming and we hit the cow. The two airbags [deployed] and I swerved back to the left to avoid the median in the road. I wasn’t even able to see what was in front of me and I stopped,” added McCatty.

On Saturday, TransJamaican Highway (TJH) Limited Chief Executive Officer Ivan Anderson told the Sunday Observer that he had received a report on the incident and raised concern about residents living along that section of the highway repeatedly cutting through the fencing to get to their homes after disembarking buses travelling along the highway.

“The fence in this location has been cut and repaired several times since the start of the year. Since the initial cutting we doubled the fencing in this location by adding hog wire to the barbed wire; it is being cut by persons coming off buses on the highway and going into the community,” Anderson said in a WhatsApp response.

He said TJH is now in the process of identifying the owner of the cow as the animal was tagged.

On September 13 last year a woman had to be rushed to hospital after cattle strayed onto the highway shortly after midnight, causing extensive damage to two vehicles, a Toyota Axio and a Toyota Tacoma, and injuring occupants.

At that time the highway was toll-free. But when TJH commenced charging on December 27, 2025 it assured motorists of a First-World roadway supported by 24-hour patrols and consistent maintenance.

“Our commitment is to deliver a safe, reliable, and efficient driving experience across this new section in a manner that is consistent with our offerings on all legs of the TransJam Highway’s network. In order to deliver these services sustainably, we will introduce a toll rate structure at both the Toll Gate-MainLine Toll Plaza and the Toll Gate-Ramp Toll Plaza,” TJH said in an Instagram post.

However, for McCatty, the issue of stray cattle was compounded by him not seeing any patrols near midnight, and for close to an hour after the collision.

“The scary part about it is that when the car hit the cow all the lights went, because the battery got dislodged completely. We were out there on the highway in complete darkness,” he said.

“I didn’t know if a truck was going to come and run straight into us; and there has been an incident before on the highway network where people died after having an accident and then an oncoming vehicle hit them,” he added.

He said he was relieved when a tow truck, en route to Mandeville, stopped at the accident scene and subsequently removed his vehicle.

“God is good, because a wrecker was passing and stopped and had on its hazard lights; that give us some sense of calm that people wouldn’t run up into us in the darkness,” he said.

“The car bonnet seemed to have cut the cow’s neck. It took us about an hour to get off the road. During that time other vehicles stopped, but we didn’t see anybody from the toll [company] patrolling,” added McCatty.

He said he returned to Clarendon the Sunday afternoon following the accident to report it.

“We filed a report at the Four Paths Police Station on Sunday afternoon, because Sunday morning I couldn’t miss church. I had to give God thanks. We came out with no wounds. I reported the accident to the insurance company and the vehicle is basically written off,” he explained.

Vice chairman of the National Road Safety Council Dr Lucien Jones said he previously engaged the National Road Operating and Constructing Company (NROCC) — which is responsible for overseeing the design, construction, and maintenance of Jamaica’s highways — about the danger of stray animals on the high-speed road.

“Having a stray animal on a road which provides for driving at a fairly high speed to enable people to get from point A to point B in a fairly short time and therefore aid in the whole transportation sector carrying goods and people across the country, poses a severe problem,” he said.

“We have had this issue before. We have had discussions about it with operators of the highway [and] NROCC. We have had remedial things done on the highway, because the primary problem, as I understand it, has to do with people breaking or stealing the wires [fencing] on the highway and thus allowing cows to enter into a guarded space,” added Jones.

He is calling for the municipal corporations across Jamaica to reinstitute animal pounds and remove stray animals from endangering road users.

“We have had discussions about the role of the owners and now to hear that there was a crash recently involving a cow and a vehicle, thank God nobody died. It again raises the issue of how well we are guarding the space across the country on the highways. Not only the East-West or the North-South, but the one going from May Pen up into Mandeville. It raises an important issue which was addressed recently in an Observer editorial,” Dr Jones said.

He argued that the municipal authorities have “a mandate to provide for and enable the leading of stray cattle into pounds and to prevent individuals from allowing this kind of very dangerous situation to continue”.

Jones pointed to statistics indicating that 214 people have died on the nation’s roads since the start of the year, compared to 242 for the corresponding period last year.

“I would once again appeal to those who are so empowered — the municipal authorities and NROCC — to make sure, either separately or jointly, that our highways are made free of any kind of animal straying onto the road,” he said.

Dr Jones also pointed to another worrying trend of motorists driving the wrong way on highways.

On August 13 Parton Buchanan, a 56-year-old resident of Blenheim district in Hanover, died in a crash after he reportedly drove the wrong way onto the Porus off-ramp section of the highway near Williamsfield.

“In those instances where people have gone off-ramp in the wrong direction, they did so to either escape paying the toll or they are not aware of [how to use] that particular part of the highway. [It] requires an increase in public education as to how in certain areas we use the highways and to get people to be aware of the dangers,” said Jones.

McCatty is hoping that another layer of safety will be added by illuminating sections of the highway.

“When you have no light out there it is completely dark. If we can have lights where the toll booths are, why can’t we have it along the toll road? I am not saying you should have lights three feet apart, but there should be more light on the road,” he said.

World.title: Take responsibility!
World.content:
An injured Moo Moo seen at the side of a section of Walks Road in Spanish Town, St Catherine, last Monday. She was euthanised last Wednesday after Veterinary Services Division professionals determined her injuries were too severe. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

JAMAICA needs more animal shelters, but livestock owners must stop abandoning their roaming, injured animals for the Government to fix, warned Dr Sophia Ramlal, director of the country’s veterinary services.

Her comments come in the wake of a recent case involving an injured cow, given the name Moo Moo by residents, that spent days at the side of a road in Spanish Town, St Catherine, after being struck by a vehicle, with no owner coming forward to claim her.

Dr Ramlal said while such cases are not common, they have occurred before and are a cause for concern given the dangers stray animals pose to motorists and the general public.

“The Cruelty to Animals Act would address basic welfare issues for animals, the Keeping of Animals Act as well, which speaks to how animals are supposed to be kept and basic things should be provided to them, et cetera. However, there is a need for more pounds in Jamaica. There is a need for the ability to move animals that are stray and ownerless. I want to say, it is usually an instance where we have animals that are ownerless, or owners are unwilling to come forward and claim the animals, as is the case with this cow [Moo Moo] I’m addressing. In those instances, there is a need for the ability to remove the animals from the space to determine what is to happen to them,” said Ramlal.

She noted that a handful of organisations are already performing work that extends beyond what their limited infrastructure can reasonably support.

“The Jamaica Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (JSPCA) does really fantastic work, but they are probably, along with a couple of other entities, they are tasked with doing almost national duties without necessarily the infrastructure, so we need to be looking at more shelters, shelters even that work during disasters,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Ramlal said the Government is actively working to tackle rising public safety risks, crop destruction, and traffic hazards caused by stray livestock and roaming animals. Most recently, the Clarendon Municipal Corporation developed a new 20-acre holding facility and retrofitted transport trucks to manage roaming cattle and stray animals.

While State intervention is paramount, Dr Ramlal made it clear that this should not be left up to the Government to assume responsibility for animals whose owners can be identified or are unwilling to come forward.

“In this recent case, yes, the Government had stepped in to mobilise the agency as a State to both treat with euthanasia as well as the disposal of the carcass. There is also the process, though, in law, that if injuries occur and the owners are found, that through the court system, a judge may determine what costs are applicable and so on and so forth. In this case [involving Moo Moo], the State had to step in to mobilise and treat with the euthanasia and the disposal of the carcass.

“It is the owner’s cost to cover. It ought to be. The journey, the treatment of the animal, the euthanasia of the animal, if the animals were moved to a pound, all of those things, it is set out in law where those costs would have to be borne by the owner,“ Ramlal told the

Sunday Observer. “But given the circumstances of this cow and given the time frame and the confirmation from the police that nobody had come forward to claim ownership of the animal, then the necessaries had to be done in really the interest of the cow to relieve pain and suffering and to treat with this matter.”

She stressed that greater partnership is needed between the Government, communities and animal owners to keep animals safe, urging the public to report instances of neglected animals as quickly as possible.

“More shelters are needed, but we also need persons who own animals to be responsible owners. They need to be kept confined, they need to be fed, they need to be watered, they need to have proper shelter, and they need to be able to live normal, happy, healthy lives,” said Ramlal.

“We are looking to update our legislation to talk about not just basic cruelty, but also how it is that all of these five freedoms can be embodied in our legislation. We talk about how animals should be kept, how they should be treated if you’re using animals for work or sport, those kinds of things are in train, as we really also want to look at strengthening the legislation,” she added.

Ramlal said the latest incident proves that more and more Jamaicans are looking out for animals and this is a welcome move.

“I think Jamaicans love animals. I think it is growing amongst us that. Look, animals are a part of our ecosystem. More and more Jamaicans are embracing what we like to call in the veterinary medical fraternity and the medical fraternity, the concept of one health. More and more, we Jamaicans see animals not just as pets, but as companions, as service animals. Jamaicans’ view on animals and their contribution to society is on a positive trajectory, and I think what we saw unfolding with this cow tells you that Jamaicans from all walks of life can appreciate that animals are living beings and that they need support and that they’re willing to jump in and roll up their sleeves and help,” said Ramlal, reminding citizens to report any incident of animal abuse or neglect.

World.title: Eager for more
World.content:
Bloom: On Earth As It Is In Heaven (2026) by Avree Walker is delivered by the NDTC during Sunday evening’s sold-out performance at Iberostar Resort in Montego Bay.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — A standing ovation and packed auditorium at Iberostar Rose Hall Resort, Sunday evening, was a signal to principals of the National Dance Theatre Company (NDTC) that Montego Bay is eager to play a larger role in its annual season of dance.

Enthralled by an evening of intense and beautifully choreographed pieces, the appreciative audience applauded heartily after each performance and were left appearing eager for more.

There were audible oohs and ahhs of amazement as members of the troupe twisted, twirled, leapt, and executed a range of intricate moves across the stage.

The show was also remarkable in that it was the first time ever in its 64-year history that the NDTC was closing its season in the second city.

As Montego Bay’s Mayor Richard Vernon explained, the show had a dual purpose: To assist local dance troupe First Dance Studios as it recovers from the impact of last October’s Hurricane Melissa and to fulfil NDTC’s Artistic Director Marlon D Simms’ long-held dream of bringing the event to St James.

“We’re happy to welcome the NDTC [to] the city of Montego Bay and I trust that this will not be, in the future, for the sake of Melissa, but for the sake of culture…” Vernon told the gathering Sunday night. “[T]his is real, sustainable and something we can look forward to.”

Also present was hotelier and Montego Bay Arts Council Chairman Josef Forstmayr, who said more of these events are needed in the western city.

“We have to work hard; Montego Bay is better than its reputation. We are not just about sun, sea, and sand. This is a place now that has a very solid demand for cultural entertainment more than reggae, and we need to make sure that we get our fair share,” he said. “As we can see tonight, we have the potential to make it a worthwhile and financially successful enterprise, and we all need to work together to get a proper theatre, to get a proper venue where we can host events of that nature; we deserve it.”

Forstmayr did not hold back in his assessment of the event.

“You can see the turnout; it’s a fantastic turnout. There is an energy here. It makes you proud and then to see world-famous choreography, Many Rivers to Cross by [Rex] Nettleford, I mean, performed exquisitely by the elite dancers, it’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience — it’s spectacular, it’s just amazing, I’m over the moon,” he said.

The production was a feast for the senses, with its striking backdrops, vibrant colours, and eye-catching costumes complementing choreography that was precisely synchronised.

“It was exciting, we were all transfixed by what was happening on-stage…[I]t was a well-executed event, and I am very happy that I came this evening and we are looking forward to more for Montego Bay,” vice-president of the Montego Bay Chamber of Commerce and Industry Nadine Spence shared.

Local architect Isiaa Madden was also among those captivated by the performance.

“I think it’s fantastic! I think this is a great addition for Montego Bay, and I hope they’ll be back soon so that I can use my Sunday evenings to come to something like this, because it was great,” she said.

The NDTC’s artistic director also hinted that the performance could mark the beginning of something bigger for the company and the city.

“Perhaps tonight is more than a historic first; perhaps it’s the beginning of a new tradition,” Simms said to roaring applause.

He went on to thank the city of Montego Bay for welcoming the company so warmly, for standing with First Dance Studios, and for showing so resoundingly that the arts have a vibrant home in western Jamaica.

The mayor touched on a long-standing challenge: The lack of a dedicated space for performances of this kind.

Fairfield Theatre now lies in ruins, leaving the city with few suitable venues.

“We have heard the call, as well, for a theatre in Montego Bay. I do not want us to take that lightly; we need it. We have many young talents and youngsters doing their bit right across Montego Bay,” Vernon said. “They need a place to express themselves on a Sunday evening like this so that the entire Montego Bay can come out and enjoy themselves.”

In a follow-up with the Jamaica Observer, Vernon explained how he believes such a facility could become a reality.

“We have property that we can use and we can look at it from two perspectives. One, we would make it be a Government approach and, two, it could be a joined-up approach with Government and private sector, and I am hoping for any of the approaches,” he said.

“At the moment we have property space to envision and to implement something like this; we just need the partnership to make it happen. We are not going to leave it at that, we are going to have the conversations with the relevant persons and see how best we can bring that into our space, because there is a need for it, not a want,” he charged.

World.title: Six years of sleepless nights
World.content:
Shakira Warmington and her son Ayoze WarmingtonPhotos: Naphtali junior

FOR Shakira Warmington, raising a child with rare genetic condition congenital hyperinsulinism has been an uphill battle peppered with sleepless nights, financial strain, fights for a place in the country’s school system, and at times, questions of whether she has the strength to keep going.

Her son, Ayoze Warmington, is just six years old with a condition that sees his pancreas making too much insulin, causing severe and dangerous drops in his blood sugar. His condition, she said, is so rare that he is the only child in Jamaica diagnosed with the disorder, which was confirmed by his medical doctor.

Shakira said her son became sick at six months old, experiencing seizures and what she described as minor strokes. However, she said it was not until he was one year old that doctors were able to identify the condition.

Since then, Ayoze’s parents have had to reshape their lives around his health.

“Having a child with a rare illness in Jamaica is very challenging for us. His care, medication, schooling — just being able to ensure that he has a normal life — it impacts my work, and we are not necessarily in a position where I can stay at home. Both of us [her and Ayoze’s father] do our nine-to-fives and we both still have to do jobs on the side in order to maintain his health,” said Shakira, who is a teacher.

She said maintaining Ayoze’s health comes at a steep cost, with the family spending approximately $100,000 or more monthly on his care, depending on his health status, while also taking care of their daughter and covering all other household expenses. Shakira said the situation had been a lot worse, as previously they had to pay $40,000 every two weeks to access the medication Ayoze needs. However, thankfully, through the Ministry of Health’s Compassionate Care Fund that cost is now fully covered for six months, providing much-needed relief.

But perhaps the most taxing associated challenge is the fact that Ayoze requires 24-hour care.

His mother told thevJamaica Observer that she uses a glucose monitor at least three times a day when he is healthy, and up to 10 times daily when he is ill. She said some days she has to stick him every hour, resulting in a lack of sleep that causes her hands to tremble due to exhaustion.

“Because he gets ill so often I have to be the one to take care of him, ensure that he’s fed correctly and he’s fed on time, because of the weight issues. He throws up a lot and so eating has to be calculated, otherwise he throws it all up — and that, too, affects the weight. He will lose five pounds in a week just like that. He will be healthy this week; next week, he’s not eating. And when he doesn’t eat, the sugar goes down, and the sugar levels have gone into the negatives sometimes,” she told thevSunday Observer.

“I am mother, counsellor, and nurse. Over the six-year period it has impacted my nerves. I shake because you have to watch him while he sleeps. He has to be fed in his sleep because, naturally, the sugars in our bodies go low while we sleep, and his are already going low so it means while he sleeps it is a high possibility that he dies in his sleep, so he has to be fed,” she said, her hands shaking as she spoke.

“We have to feed him using a syringe while he sleeps because he doesn’t want food, he wants sleep; but whether he wants it or not, he has to get it because you have to keep pumping his body with the food. There was a time when he was being fed every hour, and I’m the one feeding him every hour, so it means I’m not sleeping. I have to feed him throughout the night; I still have to wake up to go to work, function throughout the work[day], get things going, doing it all over again — and that is if he’s healthy enough,” she added.

She said the suggestion was made for her to purchase a Dexcom machine to monitor his glucose levels, but that is an extra cost they cannot afford, so she became the machine.

Beyond the home, Shakira said challenges also exist with regard to Ayoze’s access to education. She said after he completed basic school she struggled to find a primary school that would take him. She said Ayoze was rejected by 15 schools, which said they did not have the resources to facilitate him.

Thankfully, he has now been enrolled in a private school to start in September — another expense for the family. A shadow has also been approved by the Ministry of Education for her son but because the stipend for shadows is low, they had to promise the shadow more money to make the job more attractive.

Shakira also believes her son needs to be assessed for learning and psychological challenges, but after applying for the assessment to be done she said they were number 200 in line. The mother has also tried to get him registered with the Jamaica Council for Persons with Disabilities, so as to access benefits on offer, but experienced challenges.

“I can tell you that dealing with special needs in Jamaica, it edges you into insanity. I’ve gone through many stages of depression because it’s like every day I’m questioning, ‘How will I?’ There’s just always a list, and much of life is taken up by him. I don’t have a social life. I feel so alone. It really is just my family here — me, him, my daughter, his daddy, and our family.

“I’ve gone through stages of feeling as though maybe I didn’t do something as a mother, or my body didn’t do something. It takes that effect on you mentally as a parent and makes you say, ‘Oh, maybe I wasn’t enough,’ or ‘I didn’t produce enough of something, and that’s why he became ill,’ ” said Shakira.

“I have had to deal with that, telling myself that it’s not my fault, or it’s nobody’s fault why my own child is ill. It feels like we are well-rooted, good, upstanding citizens doing what we should do in our community, and when we seek to get help for our sick child, it’s hard,” a visibly exhausted Shakira told the Sunday Observer.

She said the option was presented for Ayoze to undergo surgery to remove his pancreas, but that is a cost she and his father cannot afford. She noted that the surgery is not a cure, because he would become diabetic, and she is not sure the family will be able to manage that.

Defeated, Shakira asked for help to provide her son with the best level of comfort and care. She said he currently sleeps on a mattress on the floor because she fears he will fall to the ground and hurt himself while having a seizure. She asked for assistance to get him a customised bed, install a railing in the bathroom for him to use, and financial assistance to help the family maintain his care

“I want a big bed that is comfy,” said young Ayoze.

He said he loves when his mother takes care of him but he does not like being sick because it makes him feel sad.

“I want to get better because if I get better I will be happy,” he told the Sunday Observer.

Highlighting the challenges parents often experience trying to advocate for their children, Shakira said more needs to be done to assist families with children who have special needs.

“Find out more from parents. Gather us parents who have varying challenges and various children with types of special needs and find out what our daily life looks like and how, as a government, you can put in place policies that help to keep those of us with children or family members with disabilities to have some sustainable ways to gain assistance or gain support for our children,” she appealed.

“Where a nine-to-five job is concerned, there have to be some policies and policy changes that will impact us as parents dealing with children with special needs. You have your workplace policy, but if I have a situation that impacts how I can produce or how I can function, is it that the only option for me should be that I don’t work? If I don’t work, how will I feed my family? We need to see what can be done to allow us to be able to work but also take care of and manage our children with special needs without taking on the high possibility that we either drop down at work or drop down at home,” added Shakira.

World.title: Settling the score
World.content:
Race winner Oblique Seville celebrates as he crosses the finishing line in the men’s 100m during the IAAF Diamond League athletics meeting at London stadium, in England, on July 19, 2025.

JAMAICA’S Oblique Seville and Nigeria’s Kayinsola Ajayi are set to clash in the men’s 100m on the second day of the Wanda Diamond League meeting, the Kamila Skolimowska Memorial in Silesia, Poland.

The race will give Seville another opportunity to end Ajayi’s dominance over him this season, with the Nigerian having beaten the Jamaican at the Prefontaine Classic and the London Diamond League meeting. Ajayi will be competing for the first time since finishing third in the men’s 100m at the Commonwealth Games.

The Silesia meeting is the penultimate regular-season Diamond League meeting before Thursday’s meeting in Zurich, which will be the last event before the Diamond League final in September.

Sixteen Jamaicans are set to compete on the second day following Commonwealth Games champion Romaine Beckford’s second-place finish in the men’s high jump on the opening day.

The men’s 100m will be contested over two rounds, a semi-final and final. Cameroon’s Emmanuel Eseme, who won the Commonwealth Games gold medal, is also down to compete along with a second Jamaican, Ackeem Blake, and Americans Ronnie Baker, Kenneth Bednarek, Trayvon Bromell and Christian Coleman.

The Clayton twins, Tina and Tia, as well as Brianna Lyston, are set to compete in the women’s 100m during which they will face Olympic Games champion Julien Alfred along with Americans Sha’Carri Richardson and Melissa Jefferson-Wooden.

National champion Stacey Ann Williams and Nickisha Pryce will contest the women’s 400m where they will face world leader Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic, Aaliyah Butler of the United States, Norway’s record holder Henriette Jaeger, Lieke Klaver of the Netherlands, and former world champion Salwa Eid Naser of Bahrain.

A trio of Jamaicans — Danielle Williams, Ackera Nugent and Megan Simmonds — will line up in the 100m hurdles. They will face former world record holder Kendra Harrison, Alaysha Johnson, and Rayniah Jones of the United States, as well as Poland’s Pia Skrzyszowska.

Orlando Bennett, who has already qualified for the Diamond League final and was fourth in Lausanne, Switzerland, on Friday, will contest the men’s 110m hurdles. He will face a number of athletes who also competed in Lausanne.

World leader Ja’Kobe Tharpe, who finished at the back of the field in Lausanne after hitting a hurdle, will hope to make amends while Jamal Britt, who won in Lausanne, will be looking to finish first again.

Rajindra Campbell will compete in the men’s shot put, which is not part of the Diamond League schedule, against a quality field that includes world leader Leonardo Fabbri of Italy and Americans Joe Kovacs, Jordan Geist and Roger Steen.

Lamara Distin is down for the women’s high jump where she will face Ukraine’s Yaroslava Mahuchikh; Australians Nicola Olyslagers and Eleanor Patterson; and Serbia’s Angelina Topic, all of whom have cleared 2.00m this season.

National champion Ralford Mullings and Olympic Games gold medallist Roje Stona are listed for the men’s discus throw during which world leader and Commonwealth Games champion Matthew Denny of Australia will lead the field.

Steven Richter of Germany, Mykolas Alekna of Lithuania, and Kristjan Ceh of Slovenia are also listed.

Commonwealth Games silver medallist Ackelia Smith is set for the women’s triple jump where she faces world leader Thea LaFond of Dominica; Cubans Davisleydi Velazco, Leyanis Perez-Hernandez and Liadagamis Povea; as well as Saly Sarr of Senegal.

On opening day Beckford cleared 2.29m in the men’s high jump to finish second behind Italy’s Gianmarco Tamberi, who won with 2.31m. American JuVaughn Harrison was third with 2.26m.

Beckford, who is third in the Diamond League standings and is expected to qualify for the lucrative final in September, used all three attempts to clear 2.26m and 2.29m before failing at 2.31m.

Nia Robinson, who failed to record a legal mark at the Commonwealth Games, was ninth in the women’s long jump with 6.29m (0.1m/s) after two fouls.

American Alyssa Jones won with a dramatic final-round jump of 6.98m (1.5m/s) to overtake Portugal’s Agate de Sousa, who had also jumped 6.98m (1.0m/s) in the second round. Jones won on a better second jump.

Monae Nichols of the United States was third with 6.95m (0.1m/s).

In a non-Diamond League event, Danniel Thomas-Dodd was eighth with 18.16m as American Chase Jackson won with a season’s best 20.92m. Jackson also broke her own meeting record of 20.38m, set four years ago.

Jessica Schilder of the Netherlands was second with 20.20m and Commonwealth Games champion Sarah Mitton of Canada was third with 19.34m.

World.title: The Tilemakers
World.content:
Featured tile patterns from Indigo House: Horizon (centre), and (from left) Ipanema, Sunrise, Solid, Solstice, and Leaf of Life.

The buzz…

Indigo House was founded by two friends with a shared love of design. Amber Godfrey works in architecture while Michelle Arroyave brings expertise both in project management and interiors. Godfrey was first exposed to cement tiles while working in an architecture and interiors practice in London, and Arroyave has roots in Colombia — a country with a rich cement tile tradition. Both were drawn to the character and charm that cement tiles bring to a space.

Widely used throughout Europe, Central America and parts of the Caribbean, they are rarely seen in contemporary Jamaican buildings. Together, united by a love of materials and a shared curiosity to explore texture, pattern and colour, Godfrey and Arroyave set out to design and source cement tiles that reflect the vibrancy of Jamaica and the Caribbean. Their tiles go beyond the functional, treating every surface as an opportunity for beauty and craft.

The product… Cement tiles were first manufactured in the mid-1800s, and the fabrication process has changed very little since. Each tile is handmade by skilled artisans using Portland cement, marble powder, fine sand and natural pigments — a craft with origins in Catalonia, Spain.



The process begins with a mould, which forms the framework for the tile. Pigments are carefully poured into the mould to create the pattern, before the tile is placed under a hydraulic press and compacted under high pressure. It is then cured and finished by hand.

The result is a surface that brings warmth, character and artistry to both residential and commercial spaces. Subtle variations in colour and texture are part of the charm — a celebration of the individuality inherent in anything made by hand. Cement tiles are perfect for those who value authenticity, craftsmanship and the stories told by the materials they choose.

“At Indigo House, we believe in making things with intention — tiles that are considered in their design, handcrafted, and built to last. We believe in spaces with character, joy and craft. Known for their bold patterns and enduring quality, our tiles are fully customisable. Choose from our existing catalogue of designs and select your own colours, request modifications to an existing pattern, or design something entirely from scratch — our team can even colour match to a reference image or sample. Every tile is made to order, crafted specifically for you” Amber Godfrey, co-principal, Indigo House.

Photos courtesy of The Indigo House

World.title: Scholarship announced in honour of late Miss Jamaica Universe Contestant LaToya Malcolm
World.content:
Former Miss Universe Contestant LaToya Malcolm (Photo: Miss Universe Jamaica Instagram page)

Member of Parliament and Minister of State in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright has announced the LaToya Malcolm Scholarship for Resilience in memory of the 2024 Miss Bikini Jamaica International titleholder and former Miss Universe Jamaica contestant.

The announcement came amid emotional scenes as the mother, family and friends of Malcolm wept and paid their final respects at her funeral on Saturday. Seiveright, a friend of Malcom, said the scholarship will see two high school students each receiving $100,000 to assist with their educational development.

Malcolm, 35, whose sudden passing in July shocked her family, friends and the wider entertainment and pageant communities, was remembered during the deeply emotional service as an exceptionally kind, loving and good-hearted young woman.

News of her passing also attracted international media attention, including coverage by major US entertainment outlet TMZ, reflecting the reach she had achieved beyond Jamaica.

An actress, entertainer and dance instructor with more than a decade of experience in entertainment, Malcolm competed in the 2024 Miss Universe Jamaica competition and later captured the Miss Bikini Jamaica International 2024 crown, also winning Best Figure, Best Legs and Best Condition.

Her pageant success was itself a story of resilience. Malcolm lost her father, Winston, earlier in 2024 but persevered through months of demanding fitness and dance training to capture the title, which she dedicated to his memory.

Tributes at Saturday’s service reflected not only on Malcolm’s accomplishments, but on the person behind them — a loving daughter who relatives and friends remembered for her warmth, kindness, ambition and generous spirit. Her mother, family members and friends were visibly overcome with grief as mourners gathered to celebrate a life cut painfully short.

The LaToya Malcolm Scholarship for Resilience will honour her memory by assisting young people facing challenges while pursuing their education. For this year’s award, two deserving high-school students will each receive $100,000 towards their educational development.

Seiveright said: “LaToya was special, she was loved, and she will not be forgotten. I hope this assistance in her name will give two young people an opportunity to keep pushing forward despite the challenges they may face.”

World.title: Zelenskyy: Elections would ‘tear Ukraine apart’
World.content:
His remarks come after former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov — ousted from his government role in July following a controversial reshuffle — called for elections earlier this week.

“If our partners offer us specific conditions under which elections can be held … safely, legitimately and democratically,” with the participation of soldiers on the front line and citizens who fled to other countries to escape the war, “then let’s discuss it,” Zelenskyy continued. But “it is impossible under the conditions we have right now, when Putin refuses to agree to any form of ceasefire,” he argued.

Fedorov has emerged as a rival to the current president. In a video address Tuesday, he argued that “people cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made.”

But his appeal has been criticized by both Zelenskyy allies and opposition members: Elections — which are suspended under Ukraine’s martial law, in place since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022 — would only strengthen the Kremlin’s position and sow division. “I have genuinely had, and continue to have, a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo,” the president said of Fedorov. “We have been through a lot together. “But I believe that he is either going himself – or is being pushed – toward the wrong things.”

Fedorov seems undeterred and doubled down in comments to the BBC on Sunday, saying he has a “moral right” to raise the topic of elections. “If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for?”

World.title: Man injured in drug-linked Brussels shooting after attack on police station
World.content:
The violence marked “yet another wake-up call” for the Belgian capital, the region’s Minister-President Boris Dilliès reacted on X. “We will not let organized crime take over our city,” he added.

Dilliès said his government was taking measures to address the violence, including by appointing a Brussels commissioner for drugs, who will take on the role from September, and by restricting the use of e-scooters, which he said “unfortunately, are often used by criminals.”

The city’s top prosecutor Julien Moinil said that, given the target of Friday night’s shooting, “there is a clear intent to undermine authority” — but he added that “they will not succeed.” He explained that a lot of shootings are ordered from inside prison, calling for secure zones where phones cannot operate.

A third shooting followed early Sunday morning, when a bullet hit the window of an apartment near Porte de Hal.

Brussels recorded 57 shootings in the first seven months of 2026. Two people were killed and 21 injured, according to VRT.

World.title: France to ramp up Ukraine support, says Macron
World.content:
Emmanuel Macron is seen on the steps of the Elysée Palace in Paris on July 22, 2026. | Henrique Campos/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

BRUSSELS — French President Emmanuel Macron said on Saturday that Paris will strengthen its support for Ukraine after Russia’s deadly attacks on a shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih on Friday.

Macron wrote on X that he called Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday following the strikes, which killed 16 and left 130 injured. “I informed President Zelensky that we are stepping up our support with the delivery of interceptors and are continuing our cooperation,” he said.

Confirming the phone call during which the pair discussed “first and foremost, the need for air defense,” Zelenskyy also shared on social media that the two leaders had “agreed to accelerate the delivery of the latest French equipment and missiles.”

World.title: Former EU Commissioner Siim Kallas dies at 77
World.content:
An economist by training, Kallas started his career as president of the Bank of Estonia in 1991, where he was one of the principal architects of the country’s monetary reform. In 1994, he founded the liberal-democratic Reform Party and was elected to the Estonian parliament the following year, when he became foreign affairs minister.

Kallas was also an important figure in the Baltic country’s European trajectory: After his appointment as foreign minister, he oversaw Estonia’s bid to join the EU. He was prime minister in 2002, when the country concluded negotiations to become a member and was invited to join NATO.



“I think of courage required to rebuild a state and introduce its own currency in the early 1990s, as well as the quiet conviction he brought with him to Brussels,” wrote European Parliament Roberta Metsola on social media in response to the news. “Estonia and Europe are better because of his life’s work.”



“Through his public career, [Kallas] helped shape Estonia’s EU path and key European policies,” stated the Commission.

His daughter, Kaja Kallas, was Estonia’s youngest-ever serving prime minister, holding office from 2021 to 2024. She is now the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs for Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s second term.

This story has been updated.

World.title: Thousands rally in Stockholm over climate crisis weeks ahead of general election
World.content:
More than 10,000 people marched in Stockholm, the Swedish capital, on Sunday in a protest against human-made climate change, weeks ahead of a 13 September general election where the issue is top among Swedish voters' concerns.

 

The protest comes as experts in Sweden and abroad have warned that the government's climate policy jeopardises the country's emissions-cutting goals, to reduce CO₂ emissions from transport by 70 percent from 2010 levels by 2030 and to achieve net-zero emissions by 2045.

Organised by youth and sporting groups, unions, rural associations and rights groups, the rally in the Swedish capital included Sweden's most famous climate campaigner, Greta Thunberg.

"There is absolutely no party in Sweden who are even proposing politics in line with anything close to what science says will take for us to avoid a climate disaster," Thunberg said.

"If we continue like now, we will see collapse; we are already seeing collapse," she stressed.

Another protester, Kliff Lindberg, a 21-year-old student, said he was "relieved" to see such a strong turnout. "We are so many people who are concerned about this problem," Lindberg said.

"That gives me a lot of strength, and it's beautiful to see, I think."

Since taking power in 2022, Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing government has cut petrol taxes and reduced requirements for petrol suppliers to add low-carbon alternatives to their mix.

The government has notably rejected a commission's recommendations on ways to meet the 2030 target, which included phasing out fossil fuels by hiking taxes on petrol and diesel.

Swedes will go to the polls on 13 September to elect a new parliament, with the ruling right-wing bloc trailing in opinion polls, and making a change of government likely.

According to a Verian opinion poll by the public broadcaster SVT, published on Thursday, Sweden's centre-left opposition ‌currently holds a 10-percentage-point lead over the ruling right-wing coalition

The climate crisis is very real

37% of respondents to the poll stated that the election's top priority was climate change.

The government has argued that the phase-out of fossil fuels must be gradual in order to preserve and strengthen Sweden's competitiveness and its companies.

But organisers of the demonstration argue that urgent action was needed.

"The climate crisis is very real, and it is here," said Beatrice Rindevall, head of the Swedish Society for Nature Conservation, which is co-organising Sunday's demonstration.

Citing the deadly heatwaves that have hit Europe this summer, Rindevall said, "It is time to put in place a climate policy that reduces emissions right now," according to a statement.

World.title: Sydney Marathon mishap: Munich's Allianz Arena appears on finisher medal
World.content:
In Sydney, final preparations are under way for next weekend's marathon. As the runners get ready for the race, it is the finisher medal that is unexpectedly attracting international attention. The reason: between the landmarks of the Australian metropolis, what appears to be a German football stadium has ended up on the medal.

 

The medal's design is actually meant to reflect the marathon course. "Those who look closely will discover the story of the course in the details," the organisers wrote on their official social media account.

But it is precisely in these details that the mistake lies, as the medal apparently shows Munich's Allianz Arena rather than the Allianz Stadium in Sydney, which the 42.2-kilometre marathon route passes. Social media mockery was not long in coming, with some users tagging FC Bayern in the post.

The organiser has since admitted the mix-up. "A little too much international flair has crept onto the back of the finisher medal, in the form of an incorrect depiction of the stadium," a spokesperson for the Sydney Marathon said. "We won't shy away from it – it was a regrettable mistake, even if it has certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend."

In Munich, the mix-up was taken with good humour. "Oh wow, that wasn't on our bingo card at all!" wrote the official Instagram account of the Allianz Arena.

More than 40,000 participants expected

More than 40,000 runners are expected to take part in the marathon next weekend. The flawed medals will not be exchanged before then.

"One week before the event, this is the medal our runners will receive," the Sydney Marathon spokesperson explained. "It is a beautiful medal, and now it is just that little bit more unique."

Since 2024, the Sydney Marathon has been part of the Abbott World Marathon Majors series as its seventh race. That puts the Australian metropolis alongside Berlin, London, Boston, Chicago, New York and Tokyo.

World.title: ECB head Christine Lagarde 'ready to serve' WEF, report says
World.content:
European Central Bank (ECB) chief Christine Lagarde could be set to take charge of the World Economic Forum (WEF) at some point in 2027, a Swiss newspaper has reported.

 

The Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ) reported over the weekend that Lagarde had been referred to as a "putative candidate" for the position of WEF president during a board meeting near Geneva earlier this week.

Lagarde, who is on the WEF's Board of Trustees, has thanked fellow board members for their confidence in her and said she is "ready to serve," the outlet said, citing unnamed sources.

Tharman Shanmugaratnam, the president of Singapore, is said to have led the succession discussion during the meeting and stressed that the issue should be "resolved internally," per the NZZ.

The WEF is currently co-chaired by BlackRock CEO Larry Fink and André Hoffmann, the vice chairman of Roche.

The NZZ reported that the board had not yet come to a decision on when Lagarde should take over as president, but that Fink and Hoffmann should still preside over the WEF's annual Davos meeting, which is set to take place in January.

The ECB declined to comment on the report, while the WEF did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Euronews.

Lagarde, who has been president of the ECB since 2019, is due to leave her role in October 2027 when her eight-year term draws to a close.

There has been mounting speculation over her future in recent months and whether she could leave the ECB earlier, partly fuelled by Lagarde's own comments on her possibly taking part in the upcoming French presidential election campaign.

Speaking to Euronews in July, Lagarde ruled herself out of making a run for the French presidency itself, however.

"I'm not a candidate for anything, but I'm very keen that Europe is protected, that Europe is the framework within which member states operate, including France," she said.

World.title: From Middle East to e-sports: Macron hosts Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman
World.content:
French president Emmanuel Macron is on Sunday hosting Saudi Arabia's crown prince and de facto ruler, Mohammed bin Salman, for a two-day visit whose agenda ranges from e-sports to the war in the Middle East.

 

Several agreements covering health, transport and energy are to be signed on Monday, the second day of the visit, according to an official at the French presidency, underscoring the strength of relations between Paris and Riyadh. The leaders are expected to address the "major economic and strategic issues that underpin the Franco-Saudi partnership", the Élysée said, notably in energy, aerospace and defence.

According to the Élysée, the visit "reflects the vitality of the dialogue between the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and France, and will help to strengthen the strategic partnership that binds our two countries. To that end, the President of the Republic and the crown prince will for the first time hold a meeting of the Franco-Saudi Strategic Partnership Council".

The visit will, however, get under way on a different note on Sunday evening: Emmanuel Macron will receive Saudi Arabia's strongman - known as MBS from his initials - at the closing ceremony of the e-sports World Cup being held in Paris.

Still according to the presidency, "Organised for the first time outside Saudi Arabia since it was created, the staging of this global championship in Paris testifies to France's renewed appeal as a host for major international sporting events" and "also illustrates the shared ambition of France and Saudi Arabia to make sport and culture drivers of their rapprochement".

The event, which brings together the elite of e-sports - from video games to chess - and enjoys MBS's active backing, is being held outside Saudi Arabia for the first time.

The Élysée official declined to say whether the agreements might cover the large "Dragon Ball" theme-park project, backed by a Saudi fund and under consideration in Val-d'Oise, in the Paris region.

Saudi Arabia is also preparing to host a series of major global events, including the World Expo in 2030 and, above all, the 2034 football World Cup.

Will human rights be on the agenda?

Saudi Arabia, a close ally of the United States and historically at odds with Iran, is also closely following developments within the Islamic Republic in the wake of the US-Israeli conflict.

On Monday afternoon, MBS and Emmanuel Macron will chair the first meeting of the Franco-Saudi Strategic Partnership Council.

The two leaders "will exchange views on the main regional issues, in a context that calls for close coordination between France and its Gulf partners in favour of stability and peace in the Near and Middle East", to quote once again the Élysée's wording.

It remains to be seen whether human rights will feature prominently on the agenda, some eight years after the murder and dismemberment of Saudi dissident journalist Jamal Khashoggi inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in 2018.

Related French judge opens probe into 2018 killing of Jamal Khashoggi

A United Nations investigation described Jamal Khashoggi's death as an "extrajudicial execution for which Saudi Arabia is responsible". US intelligence services concluded that MBS had "approved" the operation that led to Khashoggi's killing. Riyadh denies these accusations, blaming them on agents who acted on their own initiative.

In December 2021, Emmanuel Macron became one of the first Western leaders to meet MBS in Saudi Arabia after Khashoggi's killing. In July 2022 it was bin Salman who came to Paris - and that visit sparked fierce criticism on the left, Le Parisien (source in French) reported at the time. "On the dinner menu between Emmanuel Macron and 'MBS', the dismembered body of journalist [Jamal] Khashoggi ? (…) No ! Oil and arms !", the Green politician Yannick Jadot protested at the time. Julien Bayou, then national secretary of Europe Écologie-Les Verts, said in turn that "France is not a doormat for dictators in search of rehabilitation on the international stage".

Since then, the Saudi crown prince has made several trips to France: Saudi Arabia is too important economically and regionally for France to allow the relationship to deteriorate for long.

Ultimately, the oil factor - Riyadh is the world's leading crude exporter - especially against the backdrop of Russia's invasion of Ukraine and Europe's determination to wean itself off Kremlin fuels, has only served to seal this return to favour.

World.title: French 2027 presidential election: Glucksmann to enter the race
World.content:
The former commentator turned politician, Raphaël Glucksmann, was due to announce on Sunday evening that he will run in next year's French presidential election, joining an already crowded field of contenders, including within the left itself.

 

At 46, this former essayist and MEP, who heads the centre-left party Place publique, was expected to make his bid official in a prime-time interview on the TF1 television channel.

It was also on TF1 that, on 26 May, the 46-year-old MEP announced that he was giving himself three months "to criss-cross the country", "to propose a new patriotic contract" and "to reunite his political family" ahead of the presidential election.

While the announcement comes as no surprise and will not change much in the short term, his decision is expected to have an immediate consequence: Glucksmann's partner, journalist Léa Salamé, a leading figure on rival public channel France 2, is expected to announce that she is stepping back to avoid any conflict of interest during the campaign.

The leader of France's far right, Marine Le Pen, sees her best chance yet of capturing the Élysée in 2027 after three failed attempts, but numerous candidates from President Emmanuel Macron's centrist camp (he cannot seek another term after two stints in the Élysée), as well as from the left, have already declared their intentions.

The leader of the radical left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is also running, for a fourth time, while the head of the Greens, Marine Tondelier, is campaigning in the joint primary despite being pregnant; former Green minister Delphine Batho has announced her candidacy to ward off what she calls a "rikikisation" and a "disappearance" of environmental politics; for their part, the Socialist Party (PS) first secretary Olivier Faure and even, potentially, former Socialist president François Hollande are considering throwing their hats into the ring.

In June 2026, Le Nouvel Obs counted more than twenty-five candidacies already officially declared or claimed.

Can "Glucksmania" cross the age barrier?

Opinion polls put Raphaël Glucksmann – popular among young people, to the point that some speak of a "Glucksmania" – on 10 to 12% of voting intentions; a respectable score, but probably not enough to reach the second round.

He can also point to his 13.8% in the last European elections, where he headed a PS-Place Publique list that made him the leading figure on the left.

In order to avoid an excessive fragmentation of the vote, the Socialist Party and Place publique plan to hold a primary in October to choose a single candidate. The details of this selection process are to be finalised in the coming days and approved by the bodies of both parties next Tuesday.

Rank-and-file Socialists, consulted in early July, rejected the open primary sought by PS leader Olivier Faure, opting instead for a "closed primary", reserved for members of the PS, Place publique or a "social-democratic pole", creating a smaller electorate more favourable to Raphaël Glucksmann.

Although Glucksmann strikes a more reformist and centrist tone than the PS, he has every interest in working with this historic party and drawing on its electoral machine, as he does not have a strong enough structure of his own to support his likely candidacy.

The son of philosopher André Glucksmann, he worked between 2009 and 2013, when he was still a young idealist with unruly hair, as an adviser to Mikheil Saakashvili, the staunchly pro-Western former Georgian president. Currently imprisoned in his home country, Saakashvili was a determined opponent of Russia after the 2008 war between the two countries.

A fervent defender of Europe and a fierce opponent of the far right, Glucksmann is also a vigorous supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion and is known for his hard line on Vladimir Putin's Russia.

Born in Beirut and aged 46, Salamé had already announced that she would step down from presenting the flagship news bulletin she has anchored since 2025 if her partner ran for the presidency. Salamé, who presents the news and was initially due to return on Monday, is expected to be replaced by Jean-Baptiste Marteau, the stand-in who has been in the chair this summer.

She has nonetheless insisted that she remains objective. "I am an independent and honest journalist, a free woman," she said in February, while acknowledging that questions about their personal and professional situation were "legitimate".

World.title: Extreme weather hits Europe as wildfires, floods and storms force thousands to evacuate
World.content:
Europe continues to struggle with the consequences of extreme weather, with Serbia, Bosnia, Spain, and Poland all facing severe conditions.

 

In Serbia, the EU has sent helicopters and firefighters to support local crews battling a blaze that has engulfed more than 1,600 hectares of vegetation in the Deliblatska Pescara nature reserve, 60 kilometres east of Belgrade. The effort is also being assisted by a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 water bomber deployed since Thursday, alongside several Serbian army helicopters.

"The situation is extremely difficult," says Ivica Dacic, Serbia's Interior Minister, adding that "more than 400 people are deployed there on a daily basis."

The crisis extends further into the region, where a large fire broke out on Saturday in the border area between Bosnia and Croatia. Bosnian police closed the main highway connecting Trebinje in Bosnia to Dubrovnik in Croatia, forcing thousands of tourists to turn back and alter their holiday plans.

Several villages around the small town of Ivanica were evacuated as the flames approached homes, and local firefighters reported that some livestock was caught in the fire and burnt. Croatian firefighters from nearby Dubrovnik arrived to assist Bosnian crews in battling the forest fire, which is spreading over an area more than 16 kilometres in diameter across narrow, difficult-to-access terrain. Supported by helicopters, emergency teams continue to fight the blaze, but relentless heat and strong winds have pushed the fire further inland. The Trebinje area has not seen rain for months, leaving the parched landscape exceptionally vulnerable during one of the hottest and driest summers in recent history.

Wildfires and floods in Spain

Meanwhile, Spain has faced a weekend of contrasting weather extremes. Torrential rain and flooding in Tarragona left 11 people injured and disrupted road and rail services after more than 145 mm fell in some areas. Further strong thunderstorms are forecast across eastern and northeastern Spain, while an unusually powerful Atlantic low is bringing heavy rain to Galicia.

Elsewhere in the country, firefighters in Spain’s eastern Valencia region continued battling intense wildfires. A blaze broke out in the town of Segorbe late Thursday after a lightning strike and began spreading rapidly Friday afternoon as winds shifted, leading authorities to raise the wildfire emergency to Level 2.

Personnel from Spain’s Military Emergency Unit and local fire departments joined the response, while more than 1,000 residents from the nearby town of Gatova were forced to evacuate over fears for their homes. Supported by aerial resources, crews have since managed to stabilise the fire after it burned around 630 hectares. The events mark a sharp shift from extreme heat earlier in the week, when temperatures reached up to 44°C.

Poland struggled, but the situation is improving

Further north, severe weather has also struck Poland. Since Friday, storms have wreaked havoc across the country, with firefighters responding to more than 6,500 incidents.

The storms hit residents in many areas, forcing the precautionary evacuation of 12 scout camps amid floods and power cuts. Brigadier Karol Kroć from the State Fire Service told the Polish Press Agency that no injuries have been reported so far.

On Sunday, storms are still expected in northern Poland, as the Institute of Meteorology and Water Management has issued yellow weather warnings for two small regions, with a local forecast of heavy rainfall up to 30 litres per square metre and wind gusts of up to 70 kilometres per hour. Hail is also possible in some areas. Ho

However, the general weather in the country on Sunday has improved significantly. Therefore, the weather conditions across the rest of Poland are expected to be much calmer.

World.title: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan strengthen ties as Israel tensions rise
World.content:
Tensions between Turkey and Israel have intensified after an Israeli airstrike targeted a Syrian military airbase near the Turkish border. The strike came days after Turkey’s new military pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

Advertising

Ankara swiftly condemned Tuesday's Israeli airstrike on Syria’s Abu Duhur military airbase, 70 kilometres from its border, calling it illegal and a breach of Syrian sovereignty.

Ankara is a key ally of Syria's new authorities. Israel justified its actions, accusing Turkey of seeking to expand its military footprint in Syria, which it sees as a serious threat.

“Israel is uneasy about the Turkish presence in Syria, and Turkish ambitions to play a major role in Syria’s future are unsettling from an Israeli perspective,” explains Turkey expert Gallia Lindenstrauss of Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

“There's concern that Turkey will establish its own bases in Syria,” she added.

Israeli-Turkish tensions have risen over Israel’s war in Gaza and Lebanon, and Ankara’s support of Hamas, evolving into a broader regional rivalry.

“In general, there's uneasiness [in Israel] about Turkey's assertiveness, both in Syria and in the Mediterranean and other parts of the Middle East and the greater regional arena," said Lindenstrauss.

Landmark agreement

Earlier this month, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan made headlines by signing a landmark military accord in the Saudi city of Mecca. Known as the Mecca Accord, this alliance pledges mutual defence if any member is attacked, akin to NATO’s Article 5.

Turkish international relations expert Soli Ozel claims the impetus for the agreement is uncertainty around Washington’s willingness or ability to protect its regional allies amid ongoing tensions involving Iran.

“Undoubtedly, the United States is proving to be an increasingly unreliable partner. Countries worldwide, especially in the larger Middle East region, are looking for other ways to provide security for themselves,” said Ozel.

Iran says ‘Muslim Nato’ pact reflects retreat from US security umbrella

The Mecca Accord members view each other as bringing complementary strengths to deal with shared concerns.

"Pakistan brings military capabilities and is a nuclear power. The Saudis have the money. Turkey has a budding defence industry and a large army. It claims not to be against any country, but I think those three parties agree that Iran is a destabilising actor, as is Israel,” explained Ozel.

The Mecca Accord is set to boost defence and intelligence ties, with Saudi Arabia expected to bolster Turkey’s expanding defence sector.

But many analysts see Iran and Israel as the accord’s principal focus.

“The deal is meant to signal both to Iran and Israel that they will be isolated in the region if they continue with assertive, belligerent policies,” said Asli Aydintasbas of the United States-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey steps up as Europe's indispensable and uncomfortable defence partner

'Two axes in the Middle East'

Despite Iran’s recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, Aydintasbas argues that while the Mecca Accord has a mutual defence clause – meaning an attack on one member is an attack on all – Turkey and Pakistan will not be drawn into a conflict with Iran.

“We know that they have no desire to get involved. But it does mean there will be greater military cooperation,” said Aydintasbas.

Countering Houthi rebel attacks in the Red Sea on Saudi tankers could be the first real test of the alliance.

But Aydintasbas cautions that the Mecca Accord will not replace the US as the “ultimate security provider” for the region. Instead, it's more about burden sharing, a move that fits well with Washington’s wider agenda.

Washington has given its blessing to the accord, and expansion talks are already under way.

European Union slams 'inflammatory' Houthi Red Sea tanker attack

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hinted that Egypt could be the next member, with Turkish media reporting that Egypt’s foreign minister will join his Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani counterparts for a meeting in Istanbul later this month.

“Developments in Egypt are of major concern to Israel,” said Lindenstrauss. But she believes the Mecca Accord is an opportunity for Israel, given there are mutual concerns among its allies over the Accord.

“Israel already has very close relations with Greece, Cyprus, the United Arab Emirates and India,” she noted. "And I do envision a deepening of this relationship. And so we have the formation of two loose axes in the Greater Middle East."

World.title: Iran: President defends deal with US as best option for peace
World.content:
Iran's president has said the country's economy needs a peace deal to attract investors. The Foreign Ministry said Pakistan's top army official will visit Tehran Monday as Islamabad seeks to mediate a resolution.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday defended Tehran's expired Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the United States as the best option for ending hostilities between the two nations, which Pezeshkian described as being "neither war nor peace."

Pezeshkian said members of Iran's Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) agreed with the assessment on the basis of, "dignity, wisdom and national interest."

"There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation," Pezeshkian said in remarks published by state-run news agency IRNA. "The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path."

The MoU, signed by US President Donald Trump in June, laid out a 60-day timeline for ending the US-Israeli-led conflict as well as ensuring that Iran give up its nuclear ambitions.

The deadline passed last week with no signs of compromise by either side, and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz — which Iran closed in response to US-Israeli attacks, putting the global economy in a chokehold for the past six months — still unresolved.

On Sunday, Pezeshkian called it imperative that Iran exit this stalled phase of the conflict to unlock foreign investment to the country.

"Capital and money are extremely sensitive to risk," he said. "We have to remove this risk from the country."

US-Iran war: Will it ever end? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pakistani mediator expected in Tehran as hardliner warns neighbors not to help US

Iran's Foreign Ministry on Sunday announced that Pakistan's top military leader, Asim Munir, will travel to Iran on Monday.

The visit is part of "Pakistan's ongoing efforts to help consolidate peace and security in the region," Tehran said.

Pakistan was instrumental in getting the MoU between Washington and Tehran signed.

Earlier this month, Islamabad signed its own regional security cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, which observers read as an attempt to counter Iranian influence in the region.

Still, despite news of Munir's travels and Pezeshkian's announcement that the SNSC backs the MoU, that body's new hardline leader, Mohsen Rezaei, warned neighboring countries against aiding the US war effort, saying, "If [Trump] wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner."

Rezaei said Iran would target oil-shipping routes out of the Persian Gulf — alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz — if neighbors join the US economic war against Iran.

World.title: Could Russia's growing fuel crisis help end the Ukraine war?
World.content:
Empty pumps, long waits: Attacks on oil refineries have left Russia increasingly short of fuel. Dissident Russian economists say growing anger about shortages among ordinary Russians could help end the Ukraine war.

Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries have triggered a new fuel crisis in Russia.

Reuters news agency reports that at least 30 regions are now affected. Unlike the previous wave of shortages, which began in late May and lasted until mid-July, the current crisis is particularly affecting Moscow and the surrounding area, as is apparent from posts on social media. The gas station chains Gazprom Neft and Tatneft have already restricted the sale of fuel in the capital.

"You can't say there isn't any fuel. But it's obvious there's a crisis," says Oleg Grigorenko, editor-in-chief of the Russian independent media portal 7x7 , which Russia has branded a "foreign agent." "It's not just a personal problem if you leave the city and don't know whether you can get back again, for example. It's also an economic problem,"

Grigorenko reports that in several regions taxi drivers, courier services and the construction industry are already losing business, as many of their supply chains are fuel-dependent. "The logistics of private construction companies is heavily reliant on gasoline," Grigorenko explains.

People are also having to queue for hours at gas stations in the southern Russian region of Krasnodar, according to local media. The authorities are blaming this on a supposed increase in demand during the holiday period.

But many locals are saying that this summer season is a disaster. Real estate agent Igor Zakharchenko, from Sochi on the Black Sea coast, wrote on Instagram: "With its quiet atmosphere and leisurely pace of life, Sochi today is reminiscent of the time before the Olympic Games, when there were still not many cars on the roads and the city had far fewer holidaymakers and inhabitants. But the thing is: There's no gas in Sochi."

Poor quality fuel

Speaking on the Russian broadcaster RTVI, Igor Ananskikh, first deputy chairman of the energy committee in the Russian parliament, said he expected the gas supply situation to normalize within two to three weeks.

After waiting hours to fill up, many drivers have found their cars won't start as poor quality fuel has damaged the engine Image: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS

Economist Nikolai Korzhenevsky says this is unlikely. He left Russia in protest at Moscow's war against Ukraine and now lives abroad. In an interview with DW, he highlighted the worsening quality of fuel in Russia. Acquaintances had sent him photos of their cars displaying error messages that indicate engine damage caused by impurities in the fuel.

"The car won't start and has to go to the garage. The same people are telling me garages have waitlists of several months, even in Moscow," Korzhenevsky says. "And then you have to wait again for months for replacement parts. Obviously some vehicles can't handle the gasoline that's being put in their tanks."

He sees the ongoing problems in the oil and gas industry as harbingers of a much larger and lasting crisis.

Russia's oil exports have fallen more sharply during the war than ever before, Bloomberg news has reported. Oil production has also dropped.

"In 2019, Russia produced 11.5 million barrels per day," says Korzhenevsky. "Today it's less than 9 million. If this trend continues, and the problems with oil refining get worse, production may fall to 8 million barrels. That would create the conditions for a complete economic and systemic crisis."

He doesn't see any quick solution to these problems. In fact he sees Russia going down a similar route to Venezuela, an economy with national income in chronic decline.

Hoping for imports is illusory

The Russian authorities propose to remedy the fuel shortages with imports from India, China or other countries. But Vyacheslav Shiryaev, a Russian business journalist who also now lives abroad, says this is not viable.

Fuel distribution is being restricted due to the lack of supply Image: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS

Given Russia's current isolation, it's impossible to ensure a daily supply of 200,000 tonnes of fuel, which is the approximate amount of gasoline and diesel Russia needs every day, he told DW. Shiryaev, who publicly opposed the war in Ukraine, is also on the Russian authorities' list of so-called "foreign agents."

Another Russian economist on that list is Igor Lipsits. He told DW that the damaged refineries cannot quickly be restored and will be vulnerable to further air attacks.

This, he says, is why the authorities are already restricting fuel consumption. Municipal services vehicles — medical and rescue workers, police, firefighters — are allowed to jump the line and fill up and so are security personnel and the authorities.

"This is happening in front of people who've waited for hours and it's causing a lot of resentment," says Lipsits, a Kremlin critic who left his teaching post at the Higher School of Economics in Moscow because of increasing political pressure. He too now lives in exile in Europe.

To Lipsits, the current developments in Russia are strongly reminiscent of the collapse of the Soviet Union.

"There were special supply systems for the elite, their own shops and warehouses where they could buy everything they wanted without much difficulty, without waiting in line, and at relatively low prices. That made Russians very angry," he recounts. "When Boris Yeltsin announced that he was going to abolish these closed distribution centers, the people enthusiastically supported him. We are now in a similar situation."

Lipsits says a closed system for fuel distribution is evolving in Russia that will make it a luxury to be able to drive a car.

The key to ending the war?

The economist Shiryaev believes Ukrainian attacks on Russian targets that serve both a military and a civilian purpose could cripple the Russian economy and hasten the end of the war. He believes it would end in just a few weeks if the West supported Ukraine in doubling or tripling the intensity of its attacks.

"Ukraine could bring about disorganization and chaos in the Russian interior, resulting in a total loss of control,"Shiryaev says.

Russia’s oil empire under pressure To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

He also thinks the fuel shortage could have a decisive role in undermining the stability of Vladimir Putin's regime.

"If there's no diesel, Russia's 6,000-kilometer railway network comes to a halt," he says. "It could also cripple hundreds of factories and businesses. Without diesel, tens of thousands of trucks would be unable to run, food wouldn't get to the stores, and farmers wouldn't be able to harvest their crops."

Shiryaev says all this could result in curtailing Putin's plans to continue the war.

"If Ukraine destroys the whole oil refining infrastructure, Putin will find that, when he gives an order, it isn't implemented," the economist predicts. Everything will grind to a halt for lack of fuel.

This article was originally written in Russian.

World.title: Congo, M23 rebels agree to peace roadmap
World.content:
Negotiators representing the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels have agreed to a roadmap for peace. The US State Department, a mediator, released a joint statement.

After days of negotiations in Geneva, Switzerland, representatives from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Rwanda-backed rebel group M23 have agreed to a shared roadmap designed to facilitate peace in the DRC after years of brutal war.

The US State Department, which was involved in mediating talks alongside the African Union (AU), Switzerland and Qatar, released a statement describing the situation on Saturday evening.

The State Department said the agreement builds on a US-brokered deal signed last November in Doha, Qatar, adding that Congo and the rebels had "developed a roadmap setting out sequenced steps and timelines for negotiations under the Doha Framework Agreement."

Despite a ceasefire being in place since November 15, the shift to peace has been slow, though prisoners, for instance, were recently exchanged.

The newly agreed roadmap made clear that an observer mission monitoring the ceasefire will receive support from UN MONUSCO peacekeeping forces and that further negotiations designed to bring about lasting peace will take place soon.

How a drone strike on M23 triggered new DRC clashes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hundreds of civilians have been killed and millions displaced by fighting between the two sides since early 2022, when M23 — with backing from neighboring Rwanda — began its quest for control of resource-rich eastern Congo and its gold, cassiterite, coltan and diamonds.

M23, which is accused of committing brutal wartime atrocities, has controlled large swaths of the North and South Kivu provinces since 2025.

The State Department statement released on Saturday said both sides had thanked mediators "for their steadfast support in advancing peace and stability in eastern DRC and the broader Great Lakes region."

What does DR Congo gain with the peace deal? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
