World.title: Saudi Dissident, Held by Bulgaria Since 2021, is Freed
World.content:
A photo of Abdulrahman al-Khalid that was distributed at a demonstration calling for his release in March in Sofia.

Saudi dissident and human rights activist Abdulrahman al-Khalidi was freed on Friday, having spent almost five years in administrative detention in Bulgaria after he was designated as a threat to public security.

“Abdulrahman has just been freed following a modification of the control measure,” activist and publisher Victor Lilov. who has long campaigned for al-Khalidi’s release, confirmed to BIRN.

The Bulgarian Helsinki Committee NGO, which also confirmed al-Khalidi’s release, described his four years and ten months of custody as “one of the most prolonged cases of detention of an asylum seeker in Bulgaria”.

Al-Khalidi has been kept in detention centres in Bulgaria since October 2021 and has reportedly been subjected to beatings by police, suffered from dire living conditions and a lack of transparency over the reasons for his detention.

For most of this time, he was held in the Butmantsi Detention Centre on the outskirts of the Bulgarian capital Sofia. In January 2026 he was transferred to a temporary accommodation centre for foreigners in Lyubimets, near the border with Turkey.

“After almost five years of detention, this is an extremely important moment … Thank you for standing with me throughout all these years,” al-Khalidi wrote to supporters on Facebook as he was being transferred from Lyubimets to Sofia’s Migration Directorate.

Al-Khalidi’s lawyer, Diana Radoslavova from the Voice in Bulgaria Centre for Legal Aid, explained to BIRN that his release happened because he was about to compete the maximum term for which people can be held in migration detention, 18 months. He had previously been held in asylum detention.

Radoslavova was with al-Khalidi after he was released. She said the first thing he did was speak with his wife and children.

“He’s doing extremely surprisingly well, for me. He’s psychologically a very strong person because this is not an easy transition for him,” she said.

Al-Khalidi became politically active in Saudi Arabia around the time of the Arab Spring protests. Interviewed by BIRN in 2024, he explained that political arrests, often followed by death sentences, were frequent in late 2012 to early 2013. That is why he decided to leave the country in 2013.

He continued his activism abroad, also working as a journalist writing articles critical of the Saudi government. According to Human Rights Watch, he was part of late Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi’s movement, called the Bees Army, which sought to counter pro-Saudi government propaganda.

After leaving Saudi Arabia, he lived in exile in Qatar, Egypt and Turkey, where his wife, son and daughter still live.

In 2021 his Saudi documents were about to expire. The only way to renew them would have been to enter the Saudi embassy in Istanbul, the same embassy where Khashoggi was killed in 2018. To avoid Saudi officials, he decided to apply for asylum at the Bulgarian border. That is when Bulgarian authorities first placed him in detention in response to information passed on by the State Agency for National Security that the applicant posed a national security threat.

In April 2024, despite the Supreme Administrative Court in Sofia’s decision that he was eligible to receive asylum, the State Refugee Agency and the State Agency for National Security continued to keep him detained on the grounds that he was a threat to public security.

His case has been taken to the European Court of Human Rights, where a verdict is still awaited. In March 2026, 18 MEPs wrote an official letter to the Bulgarian government expressing concerns regarding his detention conditions and calling on Bulgaria to comply with legal decisions.

In recent years, multiple instances of Bulgaria denying asylum or deporting people under questionable conditions have come to light, as well as cases of police brutality, such as recent allegations of widespread violence against migrants being held in a detention centre in Pastrogor.

World.title: Week in Review: Momentous Moves and Dubious Intentions
World.content:
Last week Turkey adopted a momentous law on the disarmament of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). Many see the law as a major step towards ending the decades-long conflict with the Kurdish militants. In return for disarmament, the law foresees supervised release and postponed sentencing for many of those convicted of being involved in the PKK.

While the end of the conflict with the PKK would be welcome news for Turkey, many still wonder what motives are driving the ruling party and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to pursue such a deal. For many ordinary Kurds, there is still trepidation over whether they will truly see an improvement in their rights and freedoms.

World.title: EU Questions Serbia’s Turn to Russia for Help in Battling Wildfires
World.content:
After Russia sent an aircraft to assist with wildfire fighting in Serbia, the European Commission said late Thursday that it is also ready to provide assistance, but EU candidate state Serbia hasn’t yet activated the bloc’s Civil Protection mechanism.

“Should Serbia activate in the upcoming hours/days in response to wildfires, we will immediately coordinate with European partners to mobilise assistance in line with actual needs and the situation on the ground,” a European Commission spokesperson told BIRN.

There are 20 active wildfires in Serbia, Luka Causic, head of the Interior Ministry’s Department for Emergency Situations, said on Thursday. The situation is most dire in the Deliblato Sands nature reserve, which has been battling wildfires since late July.

Following a request from Serbia, the European Commission provided satellite imagery to support the response of local firefighters.

However, Serbia turned to Russia for air support. A Russian Emercom Il-76 aircraft arrived in Serbia on Wednesday evening, said Serbian Interior Minister Ivica Dacic.

“The aircraft can drop up to 42 tonnes of water in a single pass, making it one of the most powerful operational firefighting aircrafts, given that there are currently no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the EU Civil Protection Mechanism,” Dacic wrote on Instagram on Wednesday.

The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote on X on Wednesday evening that “the Serbian side appealed to Russia for assistance amid a critical wildfire situation and growing threats to populated areas”.

“Russia consistently supports the brotherly Serbian people,” it added.

However, the European Commission spokesperson declared that “relations with Russia and Putin’s regime cannot be ‘business as usual’”.

“When it comes to the support received from Russia, let us reiterate that the EU wants to count on Serbia as a reliable partner,” the spokesperson said.

On Sunday, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said that both the EU and Russia had offered to help with wildfires in Serbia, but that help was not needed at the moment.

“I would like to thank Ursula von der Leyen for the fact that she has included us on the map of countries at risk, and for ensuring that European mechanisms are monitoring the events here, meaning that we can expect assistance at any moment,” he said.

“The Russians have also offered us support and assistance, but it is not necessary at this point. We have sufficient forces, expertise and helicopters to deal with this situation ourselves,” Vucic added.

Serbia has been part of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism since 2015. Participating countries can request assistance via the mechanism when the scale of an emergency overwhelms the response capabilities of a country.

World.title: Thaci Expects Acquittal as Hague Court’s War Crimes Verdict Nears
World.content:
Hashim Thaci with co-defendant Rexhep Selimi (R) in court in The Hague, April 2023. Photo: EPA/Koen van Weel/Pool.

Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci said in an interview broadcast on Thursday evening that he anticipated being acquitted of all charges in the war crimes and crimes against humanity case against him and three other former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA leaders at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague.

The verdict in the case against Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi is expected on September 16.

“I expect to be acquitted of every charge. I have nothing to add to the arguments of the defence team or to my final statement in the courtroom,” Thaci said in the written interview with the Pristina-based broadcaster RTV Dukagjini.

The four men are accused of individual and command responsibility for crimes committed against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and in neighbouring Albania, including 102 murders. The crimes were allegedly committed during and just after the Kosovo War in 1998 and 1999.

All four defendants have pleaded not guilty.

Thaci said he did not regret supporting the creation of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers when he was in office, but said he had not expected the decision by Kosovo’s elected representatives to be “misused so brutally”.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA. It is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo.

In the interview, Thaci spoke about a 2010 report by former Swiss Council of Europe rapporteur Dick Marty, which alleged serious crimes including organ-trafficking by KLA-linked figures. The report ultimately led to the establishment of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers. Thaci claimed that its allegations were developed with the involvement of officials at the Council of Europe from Serbia and Russia – both of which oppose Kosovo’s independence.

“The freedom and the construction of Kosovo’s independence were unswallowable for Serbia and Russia. After failing to delegitimise it at the International Court of Justice [which ruled that Kosovo’s independence declaration did not violate international law], they turned to the Council of Europe. The aim was clear: to discredit the state of Kosovo,” he said.

Thaci also criticised the prosecution’s treatment of defence witnesses and evidence in his trial.

He accused prosecutors of giving greater weight to what he described as “fabricated testimony” originating from the time when Slobodan Milosevic was in power in Belgrade, and dismissing testimony from senior Western and international officials who were “the eyes and ears” in Kosovo.

“The prosecution is elevating evidence fabricated during the era of the Milosevic regime, and ignoring the testimony of senior officials from the US, NATO, Britain, the UN, the OSCE and other international institutions,” he said.

Thaci noted that the appearance of such international figures as defence witnesses demonstrated their concern about the proceedings.

“It is not easy for these personalities to sit in such a courtroom. I understood that they were seeing that something wrong was happening in this process. They felt a moral obligation to tell the truth,” he said.

Thaci declined to comment on the current Kosovo government’s approach to the Specialist Chambers.

Asked whether his rights had been violated during the proceedings, he replied that he considered the “process as a whole” to have involved violations.

He also criticised the decision not to release him on bail, saying that the arguments used against his release were based on “prejudices and hypotheses”. Thaci said several NATO member states had offered guarantees on his behalf and that he remained grateful to them.

During the trial, the prosecution attempted to prove that, as members of the KLA General Staff, they were responsible for lower-ranking fighters who committed crimes. The defence argued that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have real authority over lower-ranking KLA fighters.

Thaci resigned as Kosovo’s president in November 2020 to face the charges and together with the other three men was sent to detention in The Hague, where they have been ever since. The trial started in April 2023.

During the trial, KLA veterans and their supporters have staged protests in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague, accusing the Specialist Chambers of bias.

In 2024, Thaci was also charged with obstruction of justice, alongside four others, including former Kosovo Justice Minister Hajredin Kuci. The trial for this case started in February, days after proceedings in the war crimes and crimes against humanity trial ended. Thaci and the four others accused of obstruction of justice – Kuci, Isni Kilaj, Bashkim Smakaj and Fadil Fazliu – have denied wrongdoing.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Hungary’s Public Media News Back on Air as Magyar Marks 100 days
World.content:
Budget talks underway; location of Prague’s ‘mega-hospital’ confirmed; norovirus outbreak suspected at Czech spa

The Czech government held its first post-summer recess cabinet meeting on Monday, with the 2027 budget top of the agenda. Throughout the week, ministers have been holding one-on-one talks with Finance Minister Alena Schillerova, with many of them emerging from the closed talks with promises of budget increases for their individual portfolios. Talks are still in the preliminary stages, and the draft budget should be submitted by the government by the end of September, with the ruling ANO party flagging healthcare and transport infrastructure as its two top priorities. Looking at some of the key announcements, Defence Minister Jaromir Zuna of the far-right SPD party said he expects defence spending to increase to 191 billion Czech crowns (about 7.9 billion euros) next year, thus reaching 2 per cent of GDP in contrast to this and the previous year. On the culture front, Minister Oto Klempir said he was striving to increase his department’s budget to 20 billion crowns (around 825 million euros) in 2027. And while the Culture Ministry has long been expected to start funding directly Czech public media from January next year as the government prepares to scrap licence fees, recent statements from officials close to finance chief Schillerova suggest a new model might be chosen: specifically, that the cancellation of licence fees might first be postponed, and that the nearly 8 billion crowns intended for Czech TV and Czech Radio would come not from the Culture Ministry, but from the General Treasury Administration – a separate chapter for public expenses that are not assigned to specific ministries in advance that includes, for instance, emergency funding to deal with natural disasters.

A key campaign promise of the current government, the Czech capital’s future “mega-hospital” will be built on the grounds of the current Kralovske Vinohrady University Hospital (FNKV) in Prague, the government announced this week. “It’s not like the entire campus will be demolished, we will only use part of the campus where there’s currently unused land,” vowed Health Minister Adam Vojtech as he unveiled the wide-ranging plans for the new hospital, where some of the current FNKV departments along with those of other Prague hospitals are set to be relocated. Just weeks ago, the government commissioned the ministries of health and defence to transfer the land to the Defence Ministry by the end of August. Plans to designate the new facility as a military hospital to include the costs in reported defence expenditures – and meet NATO requirements – have been met with scepticism by some who point out that mostly civilians will be treated there, and that Prague already has the Central Military Hospital (UVN).

The Regional Hygiene Station of the Olomouc region, in eastern Czechia, confirmed four new cases of people falling ill with what initial findings suggest could be noroviruses, bringing the total number of cases to 115 patients since the start of the outbreak at the Priessnitz spa in Jesenik earlier this month. “The regional hygiene station is recording a decrease in the number of newly reported cases,” a spokeswoman said, pointing to the effectiveness of the anti-epidemic measures taken by regional authorities and the spa’s management since the first cases began emerging, and highlighting that the risk of transmission to the wider population remained low. “Within a few days we managed to prevent the spread of the infection”, meanwhile assured the spa’s director Roman Provaznik, who also criticised the spread of fake news and alarmist statements on social media about the situation at his establishment. The cause of the outbreak remains unclear to date, however, and lab examinations are still ongoing to determine how more than 100 people fell ill with intestinal flu-like symptoms.

World.title: Could Trump’s Administration Force a Deal on Bosnia’s State Property?
World.content:
As the issue of the ownership of state and defence property goes to the very core of sovereignty in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it has evaded a neat and lasting solution. For years, international interest has wavered, leaving the question to be answered at a later and hopefully more favourable date.

Today, however, with Washington increasingly driven by business motives in energy, mining and other critical infrastructure, there is mounting concern that the US could seek to drive through a settlement that is ultimately detrimental to the country’s fundamental interests.

World.title: Waste Money Wasted: The Millions of Euros Behind Albania’s Ghost Incinerators
World.content:
Garbage trucks pull up every day at the landfill that serves the Albanian capital, next to Sharra cemetery in the Erzen Valley. The pile of waste grows ever higher, sometimes catching fire and emitting clouds of pungent smoke.

It wasn’t supposed to be like this.

The promotional videos depicted a futuristic complex of two glass pyramids supported by a metal structure, where the waste would be incinerated.

Instead, nine years after the contract for the incinerator was signed, the people who said they’d build it went on trial in mid-July, accused of pocketing tens of millions of euros in public funds that should have been spent on finally solving the problem of Tirana’s waste.

Of the 12 accused, alleged masterminds Mirel Mertiri and Klodian Zoto are on the run.

World.title: ‘Return Hubs’ for Migrants Anticipated in Balkans for ‘Era of Deportations’
World.content:
The infrastructure is already there. With generous help from the EU, Balkan countries have built a network of detention and reception centres to hold migrants over the last decade. Some, including Bosnia and Serbia, already have agreements with EU members to accommodate their migrants.

“There are quite a lot of camps that are fully equipped with beds and everything needed. So, they [the currently inactive detention centres] can very easily be put in use again within 24 or 48 hours, very quickly,” said Milica Svabic, a lawyer at the Belgrade-based KlikAktiv, an NGO providing legal support to migrants and asylum seekers.

The new EU return regulations are yet to come into force. After European Council and European Parliament negotiators reached a deal on the regulations on June 1, MEPs officially adopted them on June 16. But the new rules still must be signed off by the Council of the European Union before they come into force.

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and a number of human rights organisations have strongly condemned the regulations, warning that outsourcing detention to ‘third countries’ outside the European bloc bypasses fundamental human rights protections.

However, some EU member states, such as the Netherlands, Greece, Austria, Germany and Denmark, have already started exploring arrangements with third countries. As yet, there is no official confirmation on which countries these may be.

Western European governments are under domestic political pressure, exacerbated by the surge in popularity of far-right parties, to exert much stronger control over migration and deport migrants if they have no legal basis to remain.

The European Commission told BIRN that “a few member states launched an initiative looking into return hubs earlier this year”.

“The Commission has been invited as an observer, and we are following discussions closely … The Commission is not negotiating any such agreement or arrangement,” it said in a written response.

Nicholas Ioannides, deputy minister for migration in Cyprus, which currently holds the presidency of the Council of the European Union, said in June that the plan is to set up these hubs “maybe in Africa or Asia”, but “not close to European borders”.

Some Western Balkan leaders have previously rejected the idea of hosting return hubs, most notably when Britain explored the same option with unnamed countries in the region, as the BBC reported last year.

While Kosovo’s Prime Minister Albin Kurti expressed openness towards the idea, Albania has heavily criticised the concept of return hubs, even though it has set up migrant holding camps for use by Italy. Montenegro’s Prime Minister Milojko Spajic said in October 2025 that his country will not be hosting rejected asylum seekers from Britain.

Nikola Kovacevic, a Serbian lawyer who has represented refugees for more than a decade, told BIRN that if return hubs are located in the Western Balkans, the EU will “send people who have a terrible situation, but don’t meet requirements for asylum”, while “simultaneously testing” whether the state to which they are to be returned is a safe enough.

Kovacevic argued, however, that “Serbia, as a country which cannot effectively protect the human rights of refugees and asylum seekers, is not a safe third country”.

World.title: Croatia Isn’t Facing a Fuel Shortage, But Prices Will Rise
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – Croatia isn’t facing any sort of genuine fuel shortage, but experts are warning that prices will definitely rise.

Diesel shortages aren’t a realistic threat to Croatia, but prices will very likely rise again, warns energy expert Jasminko Umičević. He sees the problem in the lack of refining capacity in Europe and disruptions in supply. Poslovni reports that energy expert Jasminko Umičević spoke about the situation on the energy market, potential shortages and price movements for HRT.

Owing to disruptions on the global oil market and supply problems, concern is growing about the availability of diesel. Energy expert Jasminko Umičević believes there is no real danger of shortages in Croatia, although prices could remain high. “I don’t think there’s any real fear that shortages will occur. I believe high prices will continue, and that is the biggest problem. Regardless of the fact that the diesel market is very tight, especially across Europe. The main reason at this moment is the Strait of Hormuz and all the problems that stem from it,” says Umičević.

He also sees a problem in the structure of European refineries, which do not have sufficient capacity to produce diesel, while Europe has significantly higher consumption of this fuel than, for example, the United States. “European refineries are under-capacitated for sufficient diesel production, because the European market is a diesel market. Today we are in a situation where Europe has reduced its refining capacity by 30 percent over the last 20 years or so. Under the motto: better to import than to produce. And these are the results now,” he stresses. An additional problem for supply is the change in the sources from which Europe obtains all of its diesel.

“Previously the main source was Russia. After the sanctions everything shifted to Arab countries. Now we have a problem with the Arab countries. And recently there have been major problems, after the Ukrainian ones, with the new tactics of destroying refineries. That’s why there is no diesel. The market is tight, it’s always like that – when supply is lower, prices are higher,” he explains.

rijeka’s refinery still isn’t operating at full capacity

For Croatia in particular, the Rijeka refinery is particularly important, but its operation was briefly disrupted on Friday by a lightning strike on a substation. Umičević believes that if the problem is only with the substation, the fault could be fixed relatively quickly, but stresses that this is a situation that should not be ignored. He added that the Rijeka refinery is in any case not yet operating at full capacity because certain tests are still expected to be completed, and it should reach full capacity next year. “Especially now, the Rijeka refinery is not operating at full capacity, because the completion of some tests is still expected. Only next year will Rijeka operate at full capacity. But what is important right now is that there is production, so we aren’t dependent on imports,” he noted.

diesel prices will probably increase again

Diesel prices could rise again from next week, Umičević believes. Although the oil price has fallen in the meantime, the diesel price has remained high and continues to rise. “I think prices will rise again next week, for a very simple reason – the diesel price is rising, as is the petrol price. What is absurd, or a paradox, is that oil prices have not risen as much as the diesel price in particular,” says Umičević. “At the beginning of the Iran-US conflict in the Strait of Hormuz the oil price was around 71 dollars per barrel, and at its highest it reached 126 dollars. The diesel price then rose from around 750 to 1,300 dollars. After the situation calmed down, oil fell to around 90, and today it is around 94 dollars, while the diesel price has remained practically the same and continues to rise,” he states.

He nevertheless expects that any price increase will not be large, but notes that the final decision also depends on the Government.

“there will be enough gas, but the price of it is another thing”

As for gas, Umičević believes that the goal of filling Croatia’s Okoli storage facility to 85 percent by the 1st of October is realistic. “A month or a month and a half ago we were at around 51 percent full. Croatia has enough gas and a relatively good mix of sources – we have the LNG terminal, domestic production (which is smaller, admittedly), and diversified other sources. I think it is realistic for Croatia to reach 85 percent,” says Umičević.

He added that one of the problems is that the gas price on the futures market is lower than the current one, so storage users do not find it profitable to buy gas now at higher prices. “The key problem is that future gas prices are lower than current ones. That’s why it doesn’t pay for storage users to buy now at high prices and later sell at lower ones. However, the Government has taken certain decisions, and HEP has been given the task of filling the storage to 85 percent,” he said.

He believes there is currently no reason for concern about gas quantities, but stresses that the question of price is something else. “There will be enough gas, just as there will be enough diesel, the only question is at what price it will be sold at. Gas prices have seriously fluctuated, and after the initial summer price increase the situation has stabilised somewhat. When everything is averaged out, there should not be a significant increase in the gas price either, especially because the state already subsidises the price,” he concluded.

World.title: German Tourists Cause Fire Inside Poreč Apartment Ending With €400,000 in Damage
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – German tourists have caused enormous damage after causing a fire inside a Poreč apartment. As if that wasn’t enough, he allegedly stuck his middle finger up at the owner after the act.

German tourists caused a fire in a Poreč apartment inside a family home two weeks ago, according to a police investigation. The fire destroyed almost the entire apartment, and owner Markica Kikić estimates the damage at around €400,000. Kikić has now revealed new details of the entire incident. Index reports that he claimed that some of the guests obstructed the firefighting efforts during the blaze and is also deeply dissatisfied with the police response. “The guests simply got in the way, obstructed and interfered with putting out the fire. In the meantime the police arrived and somehow managed to move them aside,” Kikić said.

“he was getting in my face and even stuck his middle finger up at me”

He claims that one of the guests still did not calm down even after the police arrived. “One of those people was sticking his middle finger under my nose and getting right in my face. The police were removing me from him instead of throwing him out. He wasn’t registered and had no right to be on my private property. The police removed me and gave them priority,” he alleged.

Kikić also claimed there were major shortcomings in the police’s handling of the whole situation. “Believe me, there were major failings on the part of the police. They gave them documents so they could fill in their own names, surnames and the rest themselves. They didn’t take them in. The police didn’t even take a statement from them. They signed and left,” he claimed. He considers the situation was serious enough to require a stricter police response.

“This is a criminal offence of endangering life and property. In such a case, as far as I as a layman know the law, the person has to be taken in and detained,” Kikić said.

he was coming back from the beach when he noticed the flames

As a reminder of previous reports on this bizarre incident, Kikić recounted that on returning from the beach he found the apartment in flames and was particularly shocked by the behaviour of the guests whom the police link to the outbreak of the fire. “They continued with their meal, toasting, raising glasses and bottles. They even got in our way while we were frantically buying hoses so we could try to put out the fire,” he said. He stated that this year’s tourist season is over for him and that he does not know whether he will manage to renovate the apartment even by next year. “For at least the next two years, I’m financially ruined,” he said.

The owner also described the sheer scale of the damage done by the fire inside the apartment. “The entire kitchen was handmade, from the highest-quality materials. All the furniture was high-quality, luxurious, paid for a lot of money. All of this is destroyed. This is a real catastrophe,” he said, adding that the apartment had been completely furnished and renovated. “An absolutely astronomical amount of money was invested in this. Everything was made of expensive materials, there were designer paintings inside with signatures,” he said.

the police say the fire started in the kitchen

The police investigation established that the fire broke out in the kitchen while a 44-year-old German citizen was preparing food.

“Due to the transfer of heat from the stove to the pan and then to the wooden structure, the fire spread to the rest of the apartment,” the police stated. Police suspect the 44-year-old woman of the criminal offence of endangering life and property by a generally dangerous act. The competent state attorney’s office will decide on further steps. The German family has in the meantime left Poreč, while the owner has been left to deal with the consequences of the fire.

Lawyer Zvonimir Matić earlier explained that the owner must first make a proper assessment of the damage, after which he can demand compensation from the German citizen in question. “The most important thing for them now is to make a quality assessment of the damage. After that they will submit a claim to the German citizen to compensate for the damage. If she does not do so, the owner will be able to file a lawsuit with the competent court in Poreč. It is important that the law is on their side,” Matić said.

“booking.com demanded that i pay for their alternative accommodation!”

Kikić had also hoped for help from the platform through which the apartment was booked, but claims Booking.com’s response further surprised him. “An hour later I received an email from the platform informing me that they had moved the guests to other accommodation, even to the most luxurious hotel, and that I had to pay for their accommodation,” he alleged. Booking.com earlier stated that they were checking the circumstances of the case and that the guest had been placed on the blocked users list while the check is ongoing.

Kikić claims that problems with the guests began the day after their arrival, when they started bringing additional people into the apartment. “When I tried to warn him, he simply arrogantly got in my face and said that he had booked the apartment and that they could do whatever they wanted in it,” he recounted. The owner estimates the damage to stand at around €400,000 in total.

World.title: Župa Dubrovačka – An Oasis Between Dubrovnik and Konavle
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – Župa dubrovačka, or the Parish of Dubrovnik, is an area located between Dubrovnik and Konavle, known for its beaches, peace and distinctly less hustle and bustle.

In the extreme south of Dalmatia lies an area that is often overshadowed by its famous, world-renowned neighbour. Yet no matter how powerful the shadow of Dubrovnik may be, this region stubbornly continues to tell its own (much more relaxed) story. Putni kofer writes that that story is made up of a series of “chapters” written by the local, very old villages.

ONE OF THE MOST BEAUTIFUL PARTS OF THE DUBROVNIK RIVIERA

First, let’s get better acquainted with a few basic facts. Župa dubrovačka is located between Dubrovnik and Konavle, with the border towards the latter marked by Duboka Ljuta – a place where, according to legend, fairies used to sing noisily at night to scare away newcomers and keep all the beauty just for themselves. It spans an area of around 2,300 hectares and has about six thousand inhabitants. It’s separated from the very centre of Dubrovnik by just six kilometres and sits in a firm embrace of rolling hills on one side and the sea on the other. Župa dubrovačka is called one of the most beautiful parts of the Dubrovnik Riviera.

Its history is long and dates back to around 6000–4000 BC. One of the pieces of evidence from that time – a stone tongue-shaped chisel – is still kept in the Dubrovnik Museum. Illyrians once lived here, Greeks passed through the area, and later the Romans eventually ruled it. In the 7th century, however, Župa dubrovačka came under Dubrovnik’s control. Its natural beauty had long caught the eye of the Dubrovnik nobility, who built their summer residences there.

KUPARI – THE OLDEST TOURIST RESORT

Over time, Župa dubrovačka also grew in tourism terms, attracting visitors slowly but surely. Tourism began to develop there after the First World War and experienced a boom in the 1960s and 1970s, when a series of hotels were built in the area.

In this “tourism” sense, Kupari must be mentioned. This place is cited as the oldest tourist resort in Župa dubrovačka, and the first hotel was built there in 1920. The place got its name from the Kuparica tile factory, which operated as early as the 13th century. It is also known for one of the most famous beaches near Dubrovnik, as well as for a hotel complex that stood abandoned for a long time and has now been demolished. A new hotel is supposed to rise in its place. The only thing in the complex that was not demolished is the first hotel in the history of Župa – Hotel Grand – which is protected. It is due to be restored.

SREBRENO aND MLINI

East of Kupari lies Srebreno. This ancient fishing village, which was popular among Dubrovnik nobles who built villas there, is mentioned as early as the 13th century and is today the administrative centre of the municipality. It is also considered one of the best-known bathing spots in the area, along with Soline. That settlement got its name from the salt pans. One of the most recognisable places in Župa dubrovačka, however, is pretty little Mlini. The name was not given without reason. There used to be a series of mills in the village (mlin in Croatian), of which only one has been preserved to this day. Mlini is now widely regarded as one of the best-known tourist destinations in this compact area. It’s often referred to as one of the most beautiful settlements in Župa dubrovačka.

PLAT IS KNOWN FOR ITS BEAUTIFUL COVES

Bracodbk

Plat, another place in Župa dubrovačka, lies further south, towards Konavle. It is known for its beautiful coves and beaches, and its name Plat (formerly called Belenum) is first mentioned in 1400. It is home to several interesting little churches, for example the Church of St John, which stands on the hill above the village and where so-called mammoth spruces once grew. The thickest of them had a trunk circumference of more than two metres.

The Church of Our Lady of the Assumption was guarded by huge cypresses about 21 metres tall. The giant cypresses and spruces are gone, but near the latter church there are stećci (medieval tombstones), including one that is said to be the most beautiful in the Dubrovnik area. Finally, it is certainly worth stepping a little away from the coast itself and exploring the hinterland of Župa in general, the old villages, vineyards and olive groves, and the ancient stone houses.

World.title: Split Port: Passengers Wait in 40 Degree Heat With No Shelter From Sun
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – Split Port is rapidly turning into a proverbial pizza oven as passengers have to wait in 40 degree heat with no shelter from the sun whatsoever.

At Split Port, passengers must wait to board in temperatures above 35 degrees in the shade, while on the scorching asphalt and with high humidity the perceived heat regularly exceeds 40 degrees. Lukrecija Zderic reports for Index that all of this takes place without a canopy under which people could take any form of shelter. With all the belongings they’re carrying on their journey, they must stand on the burning asphalt, exposed to the insufferable strength of the summer sun, with almost no shade available.

Parents with children, the elderly, and those waiting for the ferry try to find at least a scrap of shade under the smaller palm trees. Ferries come and go, the queues move, and passengers wait in the sun with no place to hide from the heat.

The problem becomes even greater when the catamaran or ferry is delayed and passengers don’t know exactly when it will arrive. This is precisely what happened to one of our readers, who wished to remain anonymous. With her family she had to wait in the port, in the sun and without adequate shelter, and she told Index how disappointing the whole situation was.

“It was a working day and we were supposed to travel by catamaran to Korčula. Unfortunately it was late, but that wasn’t the only problem. The biggest problem is that in Split’s port you almost have nowhere to shelter from the sun. The berths for the catamarans are far from the main, and practically the only, canopy in the port,” our interlocutor said.

“There’s often no space in the cafe or bar, and if you don’t know exactly when the catamaran will arrive or which berth it will dock at, which happens frequently, you can’t even move away to look for a shady spot. It was a heatwave, it was extremely hot, and with children it was a truly terrible experience,” the reader told us.

“if i hadn’t found shade, i’d have become unwell in the sun”

So we went to Split’s port to check whether the catamarans were late and how passengers spend their time waiting for them in the sun. Because the fact is that at the berths there is nowhere to shelter from the heat. During our arrival and the following three hours in the port, a large number of catamarans arrived and departed, and almost all of them arrived on time. The biggest delay we recorded was around ten minutes, which can hardly be called a serious delay, and it did not bother the passengers either. But what many would apparently gladly change is a simple thing – that instead of waiting on the scorching sun, they could wait for the ferry in the shade.

“It’s extremely hot, but it doesn’t bother me that much because I’m by the sea. It’s a bit inconvenient standing in the sun waiting for the ferry to Dubrovnik, so I try to find any little scrap of shade. This is more of a shadow, but it will do,” a tourist travelling to Dubrovnik told us.

“I saw that today it’s 35 degrees, and it’s the same in London, but I have to admit it’s much nicer here. Maybe because we’re on holiday, but if I hadn’t found a little shade, I would have gone crazy in the sun,” a tourist from England told us. Catamarans in Split’s City Port don’t all dock in one place; they use different berths along the operational quay. Some of them are located outside the main building of the maritime-passenger terminal. At the same time, works are underway in Split’s port on Sv. Duje Pier, where a new international maritime-passenger terminal is being built.

infrastructure upgrades – but nothing to deal with the issue of ensuring shade

Once completed, the project should take over part of the international traffic and free up Sv Duje Pier for domestic scheduled traffic, i.e. better connections between Split and the islands. But while the port infrastructure is being changed and expanded, the question remains whether the problem of protecting passengers who wait for catamarans in the open will also be solved, especially during the summer months and heatwaves.

While waiting for their catamaran, passengers try in various, and some quite inventive, ways to protect themselves from the sun. Umbrellas, caps and hats become the main defence against the scorching rays, while some hide in long sleeves and others seek refuge in the rare scraps of shade. The benches under the palm trees thus become sought-after spots, and passengers settle into every available bit of shade, however small.

“It’s very hot, we’re not used to this. We’ve put on long sleeves and are protecting ourselves with an umbrella. We hope our catamaran to Dubrovnik will arrive soon because it’s really hard to breathe here,” Japanese passengers told us. There were, however, also those who did not allow the heat to spoil their holiday mood.

“We’re from Germany and we’re only briefly in Split, and now we’re going to Hvar. We don’t have any special way of protecting ourselves from the sun; we simply try to find a little shade, although that’s not exactly easy here. We don’t want to complain – we’ve come on holiday, we’re by the sea and we’re going to one of the most beautiful islands. We won’t let a few minutes in the sun spoil our mood,” a married couple from Germany told us.

During the summer, Split Port is one of the busiest places in the city every day, yet there’s no respite from the intense heat. Back in 2024 alone, more than five million passengers passed through it on ferries and catamarans, of which more than a million on catamarans. This is a huge number of people who pass through the port every day during the season, and some of them wait for their catamarans precisely in the open, exposed to the sun and temperatures that during heatwaves exceed 35 degrees.

World.title: Meet The Croatian Fortress Constructed by Nuns
World.content:
August the 22nd, 2026 – There is a very old Croatian fortress located in central Dalmatia that was constructed by nuns. Very many families found safety and refuge there over the centuries.

Beautiful Kaštilac in Kaštel Gomilica was not erected by hardened men and labourers from the fields, it was actually built by the Split Benedictine nuns back during the 16th century. They did so precisely to protect their estates and tenant farmers, with families settling within its thick walls.

Putni kofer writes that an imposing military structure surrounded by ramparts and dense walls usually evokes images of the so-called “stronger” sex, of troops surrounding the fortress, and of leaders making wise decisions inside the protected area. Any mere mention of a woman in that picture is usually a faint figure walking the corridors, convinced that the “stronger” sex will be responsible for her protection. On the Croatian coast, however, such images don’t always hold true, especially in Dalmatia. If you happen to find yourself on the shores of Kaštela Bay, tucked between Split and Trogir, you’ll see a fortress that testifies to a completely different truth, far from the usual stereotypes.

constructed on a reef 40 metres from the shoreline…

Kaštilac in Kaštel Gomilica was actually built on a shallow sea reef about forty metres from the mainland. It has a rectangular ground plan, a defensive wall and a high tower above the entrance. It is connected to the shore by a stone arched bridge; before that, a wooden drawbridge was lowered in front of the gate, according to the St. Jerome Association’s account of the place’s history. Sea gates have been preserved on the southern wall to this day, because in those times the fortress was most often reached by boat. The entire structure was commissioned by the women’s Benedictine monastery from Split.

The nuns’ connection with this stretch of coast is almost five centuries older than the fortress itself. In 1078 King Zvonimir granted the Split Benedictines an estate in the Kaštela plain (polje). In the 12th century they built the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian there, on the foundations of an older necropolis and an early Christian building. In front of the church still stands a roughly seven-century-old sessile oak, linked to a legend about a king who rested beneath it.

benedictines from split owned the land

The estate also included a nearby village. Kozice is mentioned in documents as early as around the year 1000. Relations between the peasants and the monastery were tense enough that in 1287 they ended up in court, where the nuns were represented by Abbess Stana. For centuries, therefore, the nuns were landowners with their own tenant farmers, incomes and disputes, which explains why, in a moment of danger, they behaved like any other feudal lord of the period.

The danger arrived in the 1520s. Intense Ottoman raids drove the population from the foothills of Kozjak towards the sea, and Kozice was destroyed around 1532. The Benedictines reacted earlier. In January 1529 their representative Ludovik Cipico concluded a contract with Trogir masons Jakov Marković, Grgur Liunić and Pavle Zudenig to lay the foundations of a castle in the sea itself, at the place called Gomilica, with walls resembling those of the fortress of the Trogir nobleman Pavle Andreis Cipico.

the nuns decided to construct the fortress to protect the residents

An earlier date in this long saga is also interesting. A mid-18th-century cadastre of the Split Benedictines’ plan of the castle has been preserved, along with a note that it was founded on the 26th of January 1513 by Abbess Jakobina Grisogono. That year is probably the year of the concession, the building permit, because the first traces of actual construction appear only in 1529. Sixteen years therefore passed between the approval and the start of building.

Construction was completed in around 1545. Kaštilac measured approximately 35 by 38 metres, and sixteen families settled within its walls, according to the account of the Parish of St. Jerome. The remaining inhabitants of the destroyed villages built houses along the shore, in the shelter of the fortress, and thus the settlement that for centuries bore the name Kaštel Opatica (Castle of the Abbess) came into being. The present name Gomilica comes from the reef on which the castle stands.

daily life continues in and around the fortress to this very day

What distinguishes Kaštilac from most Dalmatian fortresses is its fate after its military purpose ended. People still live inside the walls; through a narrow passage one enters a courtyard around which houses are lined up, with laundry on the line and boats moored to the steps.

Yet the testimony to this special story of some “different” women is not highlighted on a monument or coat of arms, but has remained recorded in documents: the contract with the masons, the cadastral plan, and the list of families who entered within the walls. In other words, the fortress was not raised by lords for their own glory, but by women who had to protect their estate and the people who lived from it.

World.title: Marmosets from Croatia Transferred to Spanish Sanctuary: “They Aren’t Pets”
World.content:
August the 22nd, 2026 – Two marmosets kept as pets in Croatia have been transferred successfully to a proper Spanish sanctuary in which they can enjoy normal lives. One message has been clearly put across: They are not pets.

After having spent nearly six years in miserable captivity in Croatia, two marmosets named Mini and Rio have finally arrived at a safe Spanish sanctuary. Index reports that Animal Friends Croatia (Prijatelji životinja) attended their departure to the Spanish Primadomus sanctuary run by the Animal Advocacy and Protection (AAP) organisation, where they are currently in mandatory quarantine. The association’s statement is reported in full.

“Although at first glance this seems like a story with a happy ending, this international transfer actually exposes the lack of legal regulation and the flourishing of a dangerous black market in exotic animals in Croatia. Monkeys are sold through classified ads even though they are wild animals that are not suitable to be kept as pets. Instead of dealing with the problem only after an animal has already been acquired, we need to prevent such situations from arising in the first place,” Animal Friends Croatia said.

Mini and Rio originally arrived in Croatia from a breeder just across the border in Slovenia. An earlier attempt to send them to a sanctuary failed due to complicated CITES documentation issues. The marmosets were kept as pets with the intention of further resale through classified ads.

“these animals suffer a lot in domestic conditions”

They were taken in by Vedran Lončarić, who wanted to rescue them and find them more suitable accommodation. As there is no sanctuary for this type of animal in Croatia, in cooperation with Animal Friends Croatia he managed to arrange their transfer to the Spanish sanctuary at AAP’s expense.

“They attack, and although they’re only tiny, they can inflict serious injuries. It’s hard to even imagine their speed and intelligence,” Lončarić explained. The association confirms this and warns that ads often create a completely false picture of the needs of such animals. “Marmosets are promoted as cute little pets suitable for children. That just isn’t true, as these animals suffer deeply in domestic conditions because their specific needs for diet, temperature and space cannot possibly be met. When people can no longer control them, they release them into the wild or burden zoos, which are also not natural habitats for wild animals,” they said.

“please do not purchase exotic animals, they aren’t pets”

Animal Friends Croatia is glad that marmosets Mini and Rio are now in appropriate conditions. However, they stress that it is unacceptable that for every wild animal that ends up as a pet, a solution is only sought afterwards. Venomous snakes, wild cats, monkeys and other wild animals are neither goods nor pets.

“We’d like to call on the public not to buy exotic animals and not to support the cruel trade in living beings that can end up in unsuitable conditions or be abandoned when keeping them becomes too demanding. Anyone who has the conditions can help by adopting an abandoned dog or cat,” they emphasised. As the only systemic solution, they demand the urgent introduction of a Positive List – a list of species that have been expertly assessed as suitable to be kept as pets. Such a system would prevent some of the problems that are currently only addressed after an animal has already ended up in private ownership.

It would also reduce the black market in exotic animals by as much as 60%. They cite neighbouring Italy as a positive example, which bans the keeping of all wild animals, and note that eight EU member states already use this model. Animal Friends Croatia is therefore once again calling on the competent institutions to introduce a Positive List into Croatian legislation.

The public is therefore being invited to sign a petition for the introduction of this list at the level of the entire European Union. More information about the Positive List and the problems of keeping exotic animals as pets is available at www.prijatelji-zivotinja.hr.

World.title: American Who Bought Zagorje House for €5,000 Faces Demolition Due to Regulations
World.content:
August the 22nd, 2026 – An American citizen who purchased a Zagorje house for 5,000 euros is currently facing demolition as a result of national regulations.

Justus Reid, the popular American musician and influencer who won over the public with his story of renovating a house in Hrvatsko Zagorje bought for only €5,000, is now facing an unexpected problem. As he revealed, because of the unresolved legal status of the property, his house could be removed, and he is currently trying to find a way to legalise it and save it from demolition.

Reid explained to his followers that this is why he hadn’t been posting progress videos for some time: “The reason I haven’t shown you the house for a while is that I’m currently trying to save it from demolition.” According to him, the house, built more than 40 years ago, was never properly registered as a legal building. Poslovni reports that a few months ago, he received an official notice from the competent authorities demanding the removal of the house and the structures around it.

“According to state regulations, it shouldn’t exist at all and needs to be removed. Honestly, I didn’t even know this could be a problem when I bought the house or when I started the works,” Reid said. He notes that other houses in his village also have legalisation problems, but claims he is the only one who has received an official notice so far. Reid hopes a new legal option can help resolve the situation. He says buildings constructed before 2011 can now be registered and legalised under the new rules, and he has already submitted all the required documentation.

“I don’t know how they will react or how long it will take them to reply. It could take six months, a year, or longer. And no, I will not bribe anyone to speed up the process or get special treatment. I don’t believe in that and I consider it wrong,” he stated. Until the procedure is resolved, the house cannot get an address, which makes it difficult for him to register his residence and regulate his stay in Croatia. For this reason he has started calling the property a holiday home.

In the meantime, he has bought several other structures in the same village, including a bunker, a cabin, a tower and a shack. He has announced that he will finish renovating the bunker and temporarily move into it because he needs a building with an address.

“While I’m trying to solve the situation with the €5,000 house behind the scenes, I’ll finish this bunker and move into it. I have to, I literally need to live in a building with an address,” he said in a video. He also plans to continue posting about work on the other properties, and one of his ideas is a slide that would go down from the top of the tower. Although he admits the situation worries him, he says he is “cautiously optimistic” and does not plan to give up on his project in Croatia.

“I’ll keep doing everything I can to fix this and try to resolve everything, God willing. I won’t give up that easily,” he concluded.

World.title: Croatia Will Soon Get a New 10,000 Seat Stadium
World.content:
August the 22nd, 2026 – Croatia is soon set to get a brand new 10,000 seat stadium, with the new construction likely to boost the overall perception of sport in Slavonski Brod.

Slavonski Brod is continuing its major project to renovate and expand the Stadion kraj Save (Stadium by the Sava), home of football club NK Marsonia. Poslovni reports that the works are being carried out in stages, and according to the final vision the stadium should eventually have four modern stands and a capacity of 10,000 seated spectators.

The current primary focus is on the new section of the southern stand. The reinforced-concrete structure has been completed, the steel structure of the canopy and the roof have been installed, and work is now concentrated on the facade, installations and fitting-out of the interior spaces. A solar power plant has also been installed on the roof. The new part of the stand will cover around 840 square metres and will have 666 seats. In addition to the seating area, the building will contain media and technical staff rooms, a restaurant, police facilities, a medical point, toilets, a ticket office and a mix zone for player and coach interviews.

Interior finishing works are under way, including painting, installation of electrical equipment and fitting-out of sanitary facilities. At the same time the heating and cooling system is being completed, and the connection of the solar power plant to the public electricity grid is nearing completion.

The value of the contracted works on this section of the southern stand is just over 3.18 million euros including VAT. This forms part of a multi-year investment in the sports complex by the Sava. Earlier, a new eastern stand with a total of 1,200 seats was built, auxiliary pitches with artificial turf were arranged, and additional facilities for sports clubs were added.

According to the conceptual design, the ultimate goal is a stadium with four modern stands and a capacity of 10,000 spectators, which would give Slavonski Brod a venue ready for a significantly higher level of football. Interestingly, the infrastructure development is currently far ahead of the sporting status of the stadium’s main user. Marsonia finished last season in the 3. NL East (the fourth tier of Croatian football) and last played in the top flight in the 2003/04 season. If the project continues according to plan, in the coming years Slavonski Brod will get one of the most modern and interesting football stadiums in all of Croatia.

World.title: Estonian competitor wins Ironman Tallinn half-triathlon for 2nd straight year
World.content:
Estonian athlete Henry Räppo won the Ironman Tallinn 70.3 for the second year running. In the women's race, Italy's Marta Bernardi took victory, with Liis Kapten finishing third.

The Ironman Tallinn 70.3 is the half-distance event and followed Saturday's full Ironman.

The 28-year-old Räppo swam the 1,900 meters, biked the 90 kilometers and ran the half marathon in a total time of 3 hours, 38 minutes and 32 seconds. He was followed by Germany's Hannes Butters, who finished one minute and seven seconds behind. Italy's Enzo Bourdon crossed the line in third, nearly three minutes behind Räppo.

Among the women, Bernardi took first place with a time of 4:12.03. Kapten entered the finish straight in second place, but had given so much that she fell and surrendered the position to France's Sandra Huon (+1.05). The 20-year-old Estonian nevertheless managed to get back on her feet and crossed the line four seconds after Huon, securing an impressive third place (+1.09) as the first Estonian finisher.

In Saturday's full-distance event, France's Remi Conte took victory, while Finland's Laura Jalasto was the top woman finisher. Estonia's Kristofer Kamberg was the highest placer from the host nation in the full event.

World.title: Book of condolences opened for former prime minister Siim Kallas at Stenbock House
World.content:
A book of condolences has been opened at the Stenbock House in memory of former prime minister Siim Kallas, who passed away at the start of the weekend, aged 77.

Kallas was prime minister from 2002 to 2003, a European commissioner and vice-president of the European Commission from 2004 to 2014, and a founder member of the Reform Party. He was an architect of Estonia's monetary reform and its accession to the EU and NATO in 2004, and to the euro in 2011. He was the father of current EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas.

President Alar Karis made the first entry into the book, housed in the Angels' Hall (Ingli saal) at Stenbock House, and had earlier led tributes to Kallas, describing him as a statesman who played an important role in shaping Estonia through bold, forward-looking goals and actions.

Former prime minister Taavi Rõivas and former Bank of Estonia president Ardo Hansson were among the first to sign.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal had also paid tribute on Saturday, calling Kallas a role model and mentor who was instrumental in constructing modern Estonia.

The book of condolences is open until 5 p.m. on Sunday. It will be open for signing on weekdays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., starting Monday, until the day before Kallas' funeral. The book will then be handed over to his family.

Condolences can also be expressed online.

World.title: Estonia's Mai Narva stuns world No. 4 Zhu to win Mozambique chess tournament
World.content:
Top Estonian chess player Mai Narva defeated Chinese grandmaster Zhu Jiner in both rapid and blitz finals at the WR Women's Chess Tour event in Maputo, Mozambique.

Narva, ranked 40th in the world in women's classical chess (2405) and 40th in rapid chess (2352), beat three-time African junior champion Lina Nassr of Algeria 2–0 in the quarterfinals, then defeated five-time African women's champion Shrook Wafa of Egypt 1.5–0.5 in the semifinals.

In the final, she faced Zhu, who is ranked fourth in the world in classical chess (2550) and sixth in rapid chess (2470). Narva drew the first game playing white but won the second playing black, securing the overall victory.

WR Women's Chess Tour, Africa Leg complete — and it's a sweep!



IM Mai Narva takes the Blitz title too, beating Jiner Zhu 3–2 in the final Armageddon. Rapid and Blitz champion, same city, same week



Onto the next stop:

WR Women's Chess Tour, Europe Leg

Saint-Tropez,… pic.twitter.com/bv1MCj3Zlj — WR Chess (@wr_chess) August 22, 2026

The Estonian then went on to beat Zhu in the blitz final as well, winning 3–2.

The top two players in the combined rapid and blitz standings will earn the right to compete in the WR Women's Chess Tour series final in Stuttgart at the end of November.

World.title: Storm warnings downgraded as rain, wind linger across Estonia
World.content:
The Level 2 storm which hit Estonia on Saturday has started to subside, though strong winds and rain are still forecast for Sunday.

Heavy rain — with some locations receiving the average monthly rainfall in the space of 24 hours — and strong winds swept across Estonia over the weekend, bringing down trees, causing power outages and disrupting ferry services.

The weather warning has been downgraded to Level 1 (yellow) in western and southern Estonia as of Sunday morning. Eastern Estonia – Ida-Viru, Lääne-Viru, Järva, Jõgeva and Tartu counties – are now not subject to the warning and the weather map is showing green as of the time of writing.

Heavy rain is to continue over Estonia on Sunday morning, with 24-hour totals of 50–70 millimeters and up to 90 millimeters in some areas. These higher figures are roughly the same as the overall average rainfall for August, usually the wettest month, in Estonia.

Wind gusts reached as high as 30 meters per second on Saturday and the Rescue Board (Päästeamet) has been notified of fallen trees on roads and power lines.

Stormy weather in Tallinn on the evening of August 23. Source: Iris Tähema/ERR

The storm also left households without power: On Saturday evening, 3,410 households were without power according to Elektrilevi. As of 9 a.m. Sunday, that figure had fallen to around 2,600, though around half the outages were in southeastern Estonia.

Heavy rainfall of 50–100 millimeters overnight threatened Tallinn's sewage and drainage system, and Tallinna Vesi issued flood prevention advice, including clearing gutters, avoiding parking in flood-prone areas, and reducing water use during the rain.

Urmas Kütt, head of pipeline operations at Tallinna Vesi, noted that during and immediately after heavy rain, the public should avoid using large amounts of water to avoid placing additional strain on the wastewater system. Stormwater should not be directed into the sewer network to avoid overloading the system, and Kütt stressed people should avoid flooded basements and manholes due to electrocution and other hazards.

Rescue Board gets 250 callouts

Rescuers were called out 250 times across Estonia as a result of the storm and its effects, with western Estonia and on the western Estonian islands accounting for nearly half these: Rescuers were needed on 121 occasions in this region. Rescuers responded to 65 storm-related incidents in northern Estonia, 49 in southern Estonia and 15 in eastern Estonia. Most callouts involved removing fallen trees and branches from roads and there have been no known serious incidents nor injuries.

Ferry services were subject to cancellation during the storm but are back online as of Sunday morning. The 8.30 a.m. sailing from Rohuküla to Heltermaa (Hiiumaa) went ahead, and the 10 a.m. service in the other direction is also on schedule. No changes to the Virtsu to Kuivastu (Muhu/Saaremaa) route timetable are currently expected.

Storm drain in Tallinn on the night of August 23, 2026. Source: Iris Tähema/ERR

The storm also hit Latvia and Lithuania. Latvia's weather service issued a storm warning, outdoor events were canceled and roads were flooded in several places. In Riga, water accumulated beneath viaducts, disrupting traffic. According to Lithuanian media, at least one person was killed after being struck by a falling tree and over 150,000 households were left without power.

Trains coming from Latvia, Lithuania disrupted

The conditions in Latvia and Lithuania disrupted cross-border train schedules, with delays affecting services to both Tallinn and Tartu. "The train which departed Vilnius early this morning will arrive in Riga nearly an hour and a half behind schedule, which will also cause delays all the way to Tartu and Tallinn," Elron spokesperson Kristo Mäe said Sunday.

Mäe added that storm‑downed trees on tracks between Riga and Valga were causing further delays. Elron advises passengers to check its website for real‑time updates. In the opposite direction, trains departing Estonia for Latvia and Lithuania are currently running on schedule.



Editor's note: This piece was updated to include statistics on rescue callouts and information on train travel disruption.

World.title: Kitesurfers ride pre-storm waves ahead of tempest making landfall
World.content:
The impending arrival of Saturday's storm saw kitesurfers head out to catch the wind and the waves ahead of it making landfall.

At Lohusalu harbor west of Tallinn, enthusiasts said the pre-storm conditions were ideal for kitesurfing, also known as kiteboarding.

One of the hobbyists, Andrus, was already out at sea when the "Aktuaalne kaamera" crew arrived, and could be seen making jumps several meters high in the choppy waters.

Another, Tarmo, was still prepping his equipment. He had high hopes for a good session, but much depends on timing.

Kitesurfer at Lohusalu in Harju County. Source: ERR

"Let's put it this way: when that rain cloud [points] gets here, the wind will get gusty. If it picks up enough before the rain cloud arrives and gets nice and strong, then you can definitely have a good session. Windy weather is good weather," Tarmo explained.

The whole season has been great, he said, with good winds since spring, while fall always brings windy weather and similarly suitable conditions, Tarmo went on.

Back out of the sea, Andrus said his pulse had raced a little higher than needed, and that he now needed a rest. "The adrenaline was pumping and it's been really cool," he said.

While most kitesurfers use parachute-type kites on long lines, variants resembling windsurfing and using a sail held close to the body are also possible. Source: ERR

Andrus said he could have jumped higher, even as the wind had started to lull somewhat. He said he recommends kitesurfing to everyone. "It's a fever you can't get rid of," he noted.

As for safety, and avoiding a "kitemare," Andrus said: "If you can no longer hold onto the kite you see up there and it starts lifting you into the air without you doing anything, then it's dangerous. And usually, if there's sand on the beach and that sand starts flying, that's the first sign that you should be on the alert."

Saturday's storm came with a Level 2 warning and later picked up an intensity which would have kept even the most intrepid of kiteboarders on dry land. Felled branches and trees were seen and thousands of people were left without power.

World.title: Prime minister in Kyiv: Russia shouldn't count on us tiring of Ukraine support
World.content:
Ukraine must receive everything it needs to defend itself, Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) said as he arrived in Kyiv for an NB8 summit with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Michal is in the Ukrainian capital on Sunday and will co-chair a summit of Nordic-Baltic (NB8) and Ukrainian leaders with Zelenskyy, and will take part in events marking Ukraine's National Flag Day.

Estonia holds the NB8 presidency this year, and Michal's visit comes at a time of intensified attacks by Russia on Kyiv and Ukraine and stalled diplomatic efforts.

The visit also closely follows the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Estonian independence. "This year marks 35 years since Estonia restored its independence and Ukraine declared its independence. Both our countries secured the right to decide their own future. Today, Ukraine is defending that right on the battlefield while standing up for the freedom and security of all Europe," Michal said.

The Nordic and Baltic countries have stood with Ukraine since the first day of Russia's full-scale war of aggression, now in its fifth year. "Ukraine must receive everything it needs to defend itself and resist Russian aggression," the prime minister went on, via a press release.

He noted that "everything Ukraine needs" primarily means more air defense, more ammunition and greater investment in Ukraine's defense industry. "At the same time, we must increase pressure on Russia, strengthen sanctions and close the loopholes Russia uses to evade them," Michal added.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal is in Kyiv Sunday for national flag day and to co-chair the NB8-Ukraine meeting, along with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Source: Government Office

"We are helping Ukraine prepare for winter and protect and restore critical energy infrastructure, which remains under threat because of Russia's brutality," the head of government went on.

While in Kyiv, Michal will meet his Ukrainian counterpart, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, to discuss bilateral relations and preparations for the Ukraine Recovery Conference to be held in Tallinn in January next year.

Michal's visit also coincides with Ukraine's National Flag Day, which is marked annually on August 23.

The NB8 format brings together the Nordic countries — Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden — and the Baltic states — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania — for regular dialogue on security and regional issues. Following the summit, a joint press conference is expected to outline outcomes and new commitments, as Estonia's NB8 presidency has placed regional security and support for Ukraine at the top of the agenda.

Estonia has been one of Ukraine's strongest supporters since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, providing military aid, humanitarian assistance and political backing, while consistently calling for increased international pressure on Russia. The Reconstruction Conference in Tallinn next January will bring together international partners to coordinate Ukraine's long-term recovery, and Michal's visit continues a pattern of high-level engagement between the two countries.

Michal's visit is scheduled to last one day, with the prime minister returning to Estonia later Sunday.

The summit comes as diplomatic efforts to end the war remain stalled, with Russia insisting any deal must reflect "realities on the ground" — a reference to its control of around one-fifth of Ukrainian territory. On the battlefield, fighting has intensified, while Russia continues its long-range strikes on Ukrainian cities . Ukraine has expanded its own deep strikes inside Russia.

World.title: Minister: Russia's behavior unchanged since Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, 87 years on
World.content:
Russia's behavior has remained unchanged in the nine decades since the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact was signed, Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said.

Sunday, August 23, is Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact memorial day, marking 87 years since the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany signed the infamous deal. The pact's secret protocols carved Europe, including Estonia, into spheres of influence which paved the way for the occupation of sovereign states.

Tsahkna noted that the Soviet Union's successor state, the Russian Federation, has changed little since then. "Russia continues trying to redraw Europe's borders according to its imperial ambitions. Its refusal to accept the collapse of the Soviet Union and the fall of the communist Eastern Bloc is the root cause of today's war of aggression against Ukraine," he said. "Just as the Soviet Union ultimately failed to reshape Europe's balance of power under the MRP secret protocol, Russia's current attempt to restore its sphere of influence will fail as well," Tsahkna said via a press release.

He underscored the pact, which was built on lies and cynical geopolitics, set in motion nearly 50 years of Baltic occupation and the repression, deportation, and imprisonment of tens of thousands. "Although the Baltic Way (Baltic chain) exposed the secret protocol 37 years ago and helped us restore our independence, the consequences of those repressions still echo in almost every Estonian family," Tsahkna went on.

Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200). Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

"On MRP Memorial Day, we honor all those in Estonia and beyond who endured the brutal crimes of totalitarian and authoritarian regimes," he added, highlighting Ukraine's present-day struggles in fending off with exceptional skill and determination an invasion by a totalitarian regime. "The so-called 'special military operation' has become a costly five-year war. The front line has stalled, and in recent months Ukraine's deep strikes against Russia's critical infrastructure have generated significant strategic momentum."

"At the same time, international sanctions are having a tangible effect. Russia's economy is under strain, internal tensions are rising, and Putin has grown visibly more anxious. As long as Moscow refuses to abandon its goals, our task is to ensure that Russia's international isolation holds and support for Ukraine remains unwavering," Tsahkna added.

The minister stressed that aggression is most likely to recur when it is not met with consequences. "We must stand united to ensure that those who try to shatter peace by force and pursue their ambitions are held accountable. International crimes carry unavoidable responsibility."

The MRP was a "non-aggression" agreement signed by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union on August 23, 1939, by the foreign ministers of both regimes, Vyacheslav Molotov and Joachim von Ribbentrop. The secret protocols which carved up Central and Eastern Europe under German and Soviet spheres of influence and paved the way for World War II saw Estonia, an independent nation for over 20 years by then, placed under the Soviet sphere. The 1989 Baltic Way protest, which saw a human chain stretch from Vilnius to Tallinn, highlighted the occupation of all three Baltic states resulting from the pact on its 50th anniversary.

World.title: French triathlete wins Tallinn Ironman, Estonian 10th in record field
World.content:
Kristofer Kamberg was the top Estonian competitor, finishing 10th.

The event went ahead despite the windy conditions and Level 2 storm warning, with Conte completing the course in a time of eight hours and eight minutes.

"It's now been three years since I last finished an Ironman. It's all emotional, but I'm very happy," Conte told ERR after the race.

The race is the largest triathlon in the Baltic states and attracted a record 4,300 entrants this year, for the full triathlon on Saturday and the 70.3 half-distance on Sunday. Around 1,500 people were involved in staffing the event, whose headquarters was the Unibet Arena.

Kristofer Kamberg. Source: ERR

Chief organizer Ain-Alar Juhanson told ERR a total of 97 nations are represented in the event across all categories, with 1,900 people due to start the full race, almost as many competing in the 70.3 race, as well as 150 teams. "Those are numbers we have never seen here before," Juhanson added.

Lake Raku, just south of Tallinn, was used for the swimming stage for the first time.

The toughest part of the 226-kilometer race for the winner turned out to be the final discipline, the run. "The start of the swim was delayed a little because of fog. We started later. The bike was okay, a bit of wind, and I didn't get any rain at first. But it started raining at the beginning of the second lap of the run," Conte noted.

Kamberg completed the course in eight hours and 37 minutes, 29 minutes behind the winner, giving him 10th place. "It wasn't easy. In fact, it was hard the whole time. The weather was probably in our favor, even though it's raining, because it didn't get hot, and my first reaction is: damn, this really is hard," Kamberg said.

Ironman 70.3 Tallinn swimming stage at last year's event. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

This was only his second Ironman, and he called himself a "below-average Estonian amateur" who had not put a massive emphasis on training in the run-up to the event. In a triathlon context, his level of modest training would take up about 10–12 hours a week. "I was actually a little worried about that coming here," he continued, and, as with Conte, found the run the hardest part.

"My leg muscles started giving out midway through the run, and that was really the main reason my pace dropped off as it did," Kamberg added.

The Baltics' largest triathlon festival culminates in Tallinn on Sunday with a half-distance race, where Estonians Kaidi Kivioja and Henry Räppo defend their titles. The event is already underway at the time of writing.

Kaidi Kivioja. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

In the women's race, Kivioja is looking to repeat last year's win, and her Estonian record over the full distance at the European Championships in Germany in June bodes well for that.

"You can't just look at past results and assume that anything is guaranteed this Sunday. But I'm going to go out there and give it my best," Kivioja said, noting she took on a new coach and new training regime this year.

Some of the traffic restrictions in place Saturday will remain in place on Sunday. The 70.3 race got underway at 9.00 a.m. today.
